HOWARD BONNIER

Bray is a beautiful village about fifty kilometres west of London. A young Englishman named Howard Bonnier opened a restaurant called The Palace there about three and a half months ago. Not many people in Britain know Mr Bonnier's name yet, but he's already quite famous in France. This is because he has written in French magazines about almost all the best restaurants in that country. He's only 29 years old.
When Howard was a teenager, he often went to restaurants with his mother and father. He liked doing this so much that he decided not to buy lots of clothes and CDs; instead, he used his money to visit France and eat in good restaurants. He also bought a lot of French and English cookbooks - he says he has more than two hundred and fifty!
So why did he decide to open a restaurant? Simply because he loves cooking. Has it been an easy thing to do? He says it's expensive to start your own restaurant and it's much more difficult to cook for fifty people than to cook for your family, but he's sure he's done the right thing.

Photography

When a photographer takes a photograph, he or she makes a selection of visual information that is determined by his or her technical and aesthetic skills, personal views and experience, together with a set of social and cultural norms. And in the course of this book we shall see how these factors not only affect the style, content and expression of a photograph, but also how those images are perceived and responded to by the viewer. For example, we might consider that the casual reader of a newspaper will have an implicit understanding of the photographic images reproduced on the page. But rather than accepting the photograph at face value, we might question whether it accurately recorded the scene as it would have looked at the time. Or, in contrast, does it communicate the photographer’s point of view? Is it the precise instant recorded that is of particular importance, or should the photograph on the page be understood as a symbol to represent a state of affairs in the world?

More than a game

Sport for me has always been more than just a game. The most successful people in sport have total self-belief. You need tunnel vision if you want to succeed in sport. There’s only one route to being the best and you have to put everything else to one side. Sport is ruthless and no one else is going to do it for you. It’s sink or swim.
Sport has taught me personal discipline and determination, but it can also teach you the benefits of working as one of a team. My sport allows and encourages you to excel individually, yet it is a team game and you have to balance these two aspects. It’s very much like life - you can succeed as an individual, but you must never forget there are others around you.
Sport has given me a great deal - and not just financially. It has opened doors for me and opened my eyes, and I’ve seen things around the world that others will never see. But you also have to give up a lot for those perks.

Tuning in

Some experiences etch themselves so sharply on our memory that they form islands of clarity in our recollection. For me, such a momentous occasion took place one night in California many years ago, when I lay awake listening to the rapturous strains of a mockingbird singing from an invisible location in one of the tall trees that were dotted around the suburban neighbourhood. I don’t suffer from insomnia - it was the exquisite artistry of the singer that kept me awake. As I followed his intricately woven melodies, I found myself drawn into an unexpected aesthetic environment. In order to follow the patterns that issued from the bird, I had to call on my experience of jazz and Indian classical music. The bird had me convinced that I was being treated to an ad lib performance of the most breathtaking improvisational acrobatics. I groaned and I cheered as one improbable musical variation followed another through the open window where I lay listening, until finally I fell asleep.

Fotografie

Als een fotograaf een foto maakt, maakt hij of zij een selectie van visuele informatie die wordt bepaald door zijn of haar technische en esthetische vaardigheden, persoonlijke opvattingen en ervaring, samen met een reeks sociale en culturele normen. En in de loop van dit boek zullen we zien hoe deze factoren niet alleen van invloed zijn op de stijl, inhoud en expressie van een foto, maar ook op de manier waarop die beelden worden waargenomen en beantwoord door de kijker. We kunnen bijvoorbeeld aannemen dat de gemiddelde lezer van een krant een impliciet begrip heeft van de fotografische beelden die op de pagina worden weergegeven. Maar in plaats van de foto op waarde te schatten, kunnen we ons afvragen of deze foto de scène nauwkeurig heeft vastgelegd zoals deze op dat moment zou hebben gezien. Of, in tegenstelling, communiceert de foto de fotograaf's standpunt? Is het de precieze opname die op dat moment plaatsvond die van belang is, of moet de foto op de pagina worden begrepen als een symbool om een staat van zaken in de wereld te vertegenwoordigen?

results.tgt_text:
Photographie

Lorsqu'un photographe prend une photo, il ou elle fait une sélection d'informations visuelles qui est déterminée par ses compétences techniques et esthétiques, ses points de vue et expériences personnels, ainsi que par un ensemble de normes sociales et culturelles. Et au cours de ce livre, nous verrons comment ces facteurs non seulement affectent le style, le contenu et l'expression d'une photo, mais aussi la façon dont ces images sont perçues et réagi par le spectateur. Par exemple, nous pouvons considérer que le lecteur occasionnel d'un journal aura une compréhension implicite des images photographiques reproduites sur la page. Mais au lieu d'accepter la photo à sa valeur intrinsèque, nous pouvons nous demander si elle a enregistré la scène telle qu'elle aurait pu être vue à l'époque. Ou, en opposition, communique-t-elle le point de vue du photographe? Est-ce l'instant précis enregistré qui est particulièrement important, ou la photo sur la page doit-elle être comprise comme un symbole pour représenter un état des choses dans le monde?

Plus qu'un jeu

Le sport pour moi a toujours été plus qu'un simple jeu. Les personnes les plus réussies dans le sport ont une confiance totale en elles-mêmes. Vous avez besoin d'une vision de tunnel si vous voulez réussir dans le sport. Il n'y a qu'une seule voie pour devenir le meilleur et vous devez mettre de côté tout le reste. Le sport est impitoyable et personne d'autre ne fera cela pour vous. C'est noyade ou survie.
Le sport m'a apporté beaucoup - et pas seulement financièrement. Il m'a ouvert des portes et m'a ouvert les yeux, et j'ai vu des choses autour du monde que d'autres ne verront jamais. Mais vous devez également donner beaucoup pour ces avantages.

S'accorder

Certaines expériences se gravent si nettement dans notre mémoire qu'elles forment des îlots de clarté dans notre souvenir. Pour moi, une occasion si importante a eu lieu une nuit en Californie il y a de nombreuses années, lorsque je me suis couché en écoutant les mélodies raffinées d'un roitelet chantant depuis un emplacement invisible dans l'un des arbres hauts qui étaient parsemés autour du quartier résidentiel. Je ne souffre pas d'insomnie - c'était l'artisanat raffiné du chanteur qui m'a gardé éveillé. Alors que je suivais ses mélodies tissées avec soin, je me suis retrouvé entraîné dans un environnement esthétique inattendu. Afin de suivre les modèles qui émanaient du chanteur, j'ai dû faire appel à mon expérience du jazz et de la musique classique indienne. Le chanteur m'avait convaincu que j'étais traité à une performance d'improvisation acrobatique des plus étonnantes. J'ai grogné et j'ai applaudi à mesure que l'une des variantes improbables de la musique suivait l'autre par la fenêtre ouverte où je me trouvais, jusqu'à ce que finalement je me suis endormi.

I also moved some guns and other things to this bigger cave. I wanted to have guns near me when I was at my country house. I was more intelligent than 500 cannibals !
Every morning, I took some guns and walked about three miles to my place on the hill. I watched and waited for the cannibals. But nobody came. Nothing happened. I watched every morning for months, but I didn't see anybody.
Then I went back to my old life and looked for food in the mornings. I didn't visit that hill for a long time. I tried to forget about the mark on the beach and the bones. I tried, but I couldn't forget.
It was now the end of the summer of my twenty-third year on this island. I had a lot of work in my garden. I looked at the corn every morning very early. One morning, before it was light, I saw a fire on the beach. It was about two miles away, near the hill. I ran quickly to the hill and looked for the fire.
I saw nine men on the beach below me. They wore no clothes. They sat round a small fire. The weather was very hot, so the fire was for food. They danced - they moved their arms and legs quickly up and down. After an hour, the water in the sea was high on the beach. The nine men got into their boats and began to leave.
I ran back to my cave for my gun. When I came to the hill again, I saw their two boats on the sea. Then I saw three other boats. The five boats went north.

Hi, Dad. Your supper's in the kitchen.'
John's sixteen-year-old daughter, Christine, was sitting at the table doing her homework. His son Andrew, who was thirteen, was watching television.
'Thanks, Christine,' John said. 'I'm sorry I'm late. Is everything OK?'
'Fine, thanks.' Christine gave him a quick smile, then got on with her work. John got his food from the kitchen, Fried fish and chips. The food was dry and didn't taste very good. But he didn't say anything about that. John was not a good cook himself and his children were no better. His wife had been a good cook, he remembered.
John tried to eat the terrible supper and looked around the small, miserable flat. The furniture was twenty years old, the wallpaper and carpets were cheap and dirty. The rooms were all small, and he could see no trees or gardens from the windows - just the lights from hundreds of other flats. And there were books, clothes, and newspapers on the floor.
Once, when his wife had been alive, he had had a fine house. A beautiful big house in the country, with a large garden. They had had lots of new furniture, two cars, expensive holidays - everything they needed. He had had a good job. They hadn't needed to think about money. And then he had started the boat-building company, and his luck had ended.
When Rachel had died, John had been terribly unhappy - much too unhappy to think about business. A few months later his company had closed, and he had lost all his money. John had had to sell his beautiful house in the country, and move to this miserable flat.

results.src_text:
Volunteer tourism 

Four academic writers discuss the topic of international voluntary work. 
 
A.
It is hard to argue that the actual contribution to development amounts to a great deal directly. Whilst volunteer tourists can get involved in building homes or schools, they have usually paid a significant fee for the opportunity to be involved in this work: money that, if donated to a local community directly, could potentially pay for a greater amount of labour than the individual volunteer could ever hope to provide. This is especially so in the case of gap years, in which the level of technical skill or professional experience required of volunteers is negligible. Hence, it is unsurprising that many academic studies allude to the moral issue of whether gap year volunteering is principally motivated by altruism – a desire to benefit the society visited – or whether young people aim to generate ‘cultural capital’ which benefits them in their careers. However, the projects may play a role in developing people who will, in the course of their careers and lives, act ethically in favour of those less well-off. 

B.
Volunteering may lead to greater international understanding; enhanced ability to solve conflicts; widespread and democratic participation in global affairs through global civic society organisations; and growth of international social networks among ordinary people. In this scenario, the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, an outcome where benefits accrue to volunteers and host communities, and contribute to the global greater good. However, if volunteering is largely limited to individuals of means from wealthier areas of the world, it may give these privileged volunteers an international perspective, and a career boost, but it will do little for people and communities who currently lack access to international voluntary work. Those who volunteer will continue to reap its benefits, using host organisations and host communities as a rung on the ladder of personal advancement. 

C.
At its worst, international volunteering can be imperialist, paternalistic charity, volunteer tourism, or a self-serving quest for career and personal development on the part of well-off Westerners. Or it can be straightforward provision of technical assistance for international development. At its best, international volunteering brings benefits (and costs) to individual volunteers and the organisations within which they work, at the same time as providing the space for an exchange of technical skills, knowledge, and cross-cultural experience in developing communities. Most significantly, volunteering can raise awareness of, and a lifelong commitment to combating, existing unequal power relations and deep-seated causes of poverty, injustice, and unsustainable development. 
 
 
D.
Volunteer tourism seems to fit well with the growth of life strategies to help others. Such limited strategies, aimed at a humble ‘making a difference’, can appear positive and attractive in an anti-political climate. The personal element appears positive – it bypasses big government and eschews big business. Yet it also bypasses the democratic imperative of representative government and reduces development to individual acts of charity, most often ones that seek to work around rather than transform the situations of poor, rural societies. Cynicism at the act of volunteering is certainly misplaced. The act of volunteer tourism may involve only simple, commendable charity. However, where volunteer tourism is talked up as sustainable development and the marketing of the gap-year companies merges into development thinking, this is symptomatic of a degradation of the discourse of development. The politics of volunteer tourism represents a retreat from a social understanding of global inequalities and the poverty lived by so many in the developing word.

A.
Het is moeilijk te ontkennen dat de daadwerkelijke bijdrage aan ontwikkeling niet direct groot is. Terwijl vrijwilligers op vakantie kunnen helpen bij het bouwen van huizen of scholen, hebben ze meestal een aanzienlijke vergoeding betaald voor de mogelijkheid om aan deze werkzaamheden te mogen deelnemen: geld dat, als het rechtstreeks aan een lokale gemeenschap wordt geschonken, mogelijk meer arbeidskracht kan genereren dan de individuele vrijwilliger ooit zou kunnen leveren. Dit geldt met name voor de zogenaamde 'gap year', waarbij de vereiste technische vaardigheden of beroepservaring van vrijwilligers verwaarloosbaar is. Daarom is het niet verrassend dat veel academische studies verwijzen naar de morele kwestie of vrijwilligerswerk tijdens een 'gap year' voornamelijk wordt gemotiveerd door altruïsme - een verlangen om de bezochte samenleving te helpen - of of jonge mensen proberen 'culturele kapitaal' op te bouwen dat hen in hun carrière en leven ten goede komt.

B.
Vrijwilligerswerk kan leiden tot meer internationale begrip, verbeterde vaardigheden om conflicten op te lossen, brede en democratische deelname aan wereldwijde aangelegenheden via mondiale civiele maatschappijorganisaties en de groei van internationale sociale netwerken tussen gewone mensen. In dit scenario is het geheel groter dan de som van de delen, een uitkomst waarbij voordelen worden behaald voor vrijwilligers en gastgemeenschappen en bijdragen aan het algemeen belang op wereldschaal. Als vrijwilligerswerk echter grotendeels beperkt blijft tot individuen met middelen uit welvarende gebieden van de wereld, geeft dit deze bevoorrechte vrijwilligers een internationaal perspectief en een carrièreboost, maar doet het weinig voor mensen en gemeenschappen die momenteel geen toegang hebben tot vrijwilligerswerk in het buitenland. Degenen die vrijwilligerswerk doen zullen hiervan de voordelen blijven plukken, en organisaties en gastgemeenschappen gebruiken als een springplank voor persoonlijke vooruitgang.

C.
Het slechtste dat internationale vrijwilligerswerk kan zijn, is imperialistisch, paternalistisch liefdadigheidswerk, vrijwilligersvakantie of een zelfzuchtige zoektocht naar carrière- en persoonlijke ontwikkeling voor de welvarende westerlingen. Of het kan eenvoudigweg technische bijstand voor internationale ontwikkeling zijn. In het beste geval brengt internationaal vrijwilligerswerk voordelen (en kosten) met zich mee voor individuele vrijwilligers en de organisaties waarin ze werken, terwijl tegelijkertijd de ruimte wordt gecreëerd voor een uitwisseling van technische vaardigheden, kennis en ervaring in de ontwikkelende gemeenschappen. Het belangrijkste is dat vrijwilligerswerk de bewustwording en een levenslange toewijding kan vergroten aan het bestrijden van bestaande ongelijke machtsverhoudingen en diepgewortelde oorzaken van armoede, onrecht en onduurzame ontwikkeling.

D.
Vrijwilligersvakantie past goed bij de groei van levensstrategieën om anderen te helpen. Dergelijke beperkte strategieën, die gericht zijn op een bescheiden 'een verschil maken', kunnen positief en aantrekkelijk lijken in een antipolitiek klimaat. De persoonlijke kant lijkt positief - het omzeilt de grote overheid en vermijdt het grote bedrijfsleven. Maar het omzeilt ook de democratische plicht van een representatieve overheid en vermindert ontwikkeling tot individuele handelingen van liefdadigheid, meestal handelingen die proberen om de situatie van arme, plattelandsgemeenschappen om te springen in plaats van deze te transformeren. Cynisme over vrijwilligerswerk is zeker misplaatst. Het kan alleen eenvoudige, lovenswaardige liefdadigheid omvatten. Maar waar vrijwilligersvakantie wordt gepromoot als duurzame ontwikkeling en de marketing van de bedrijven die gap-years aanbieden in de ontwikkelingsdenken samenvloeit, is dit een symptoom van een degradatie van de ontwikkelingsdiscussie. De politiek van vrijwilligersvakantie vertegenwoordigt een terugtrekking uit een maatschappelijk begrip van wereldwijde ongelijkheden en de armoede die zoveel mensen in de ontwikkelingslanden leven.

results.tgt_text:
Voyage de volontariat

Quatre auteurs universitaires discutent du thème du travail volontaire international.

A.
Il est difficile de prétendre que la contribution réelle au développement représente beaucoup directement. Bien que les touristes volontaires puissent participer à la construction de maisons ou d'écoles, ils ont généralement payé une somme importante pour l'opportunité de participer à ce travail : de l'argent qui, s'il était directement versé à une communauté locale, pourrait potentiellement payer pour un plus grand montant de travail que le volontaire individuel ne pourrait jamais espérer fournir. C'est particulièrement vrai dans le cas des années de transition, dans lesquels le niveau de compétence technique ou d'expérience professionnelle requis des volontaires est négligeable. Par conséquent, il n'est pas surprenant que de nombreux études universitaires font référence à la question morale de savoir si le volontariat des années de transition est principalement motivé par l'altruisme - un désir de bénéficier à la société visitée - ou si les jeunes cherchent à générer un « capital culturel » qui profite à leur carrière. Cependant, les projets peuvent jouer un rôle dans le développement de personnes qui, au cours de leur carrière et de leur vie, agiront éthiquement en faveur des personnes moins fortunées.

B.
Le volontariat peut conduire à une meilleure compréhension internationale ; une capacité améliorée de résoudre les conflits ; une participation large et démocratique aux affaires mondiales par le biais d'organisations de la société civile mondiale ; et la croissance de réseaux sociaux internationaux parmi les personnes ordinaires. Dans ce scénario, l'ensemble est supérieur à la somme de ses parties, un résultat où les bénéfices s'accumulent pour les volontaires et les communautés hôtes, et contribuent au bien commun mondial. Toutefois, si le volontariat est largement limité aux personnes aisées des régions plus riches du monde, il peut donner à ces volontaires privilégiés une perspective internationale, et un coup de pouce pour leur carrière, mais il n'apportera rien aux personnes et aux communautés qui manquent actuellement d'accès au travail bénévole international. Ceux qui font du volontariat continueront à en tirer des avantages, en utilisant les organisations hôtes et les communautés hôtes comme un échelon de progression dans leur avancement personnel.

C.
Dans le pire des cas, le volontariat international peut être impérialiste, caritatif paternaliste, tourisme de volontariat, ou une quête égoïste de développement personnel pour les privilégiés occidentaux. Ou il peut s'agir d'une fourniture pure et simple d'assistance technique pour le développement international. Au mieux, le volontariat international apporte des avantages (et des coûts) aux volontaires individuels et aux organisations au sein desquelles ils travaillent, tout en fournissant l'espace pour un échange de compétences techniques, de connaissances et d'expérience interculturelle dans les communautés en développement. Le plus important est que le volontariat peut sensibiliser aux causes profondes de la pauvreté, de l'injustice et du développement non durable, et susciter une détermination à vie à les combattre.

D.
Le tourisme de volontariat semble convenir bien à la croissance des stratégies de vie pour aider les autres. Ces stratégies limitées, visant un humble « faire une différence », peuvent sembler positives et attrayantes dans un climat anti-politique. L'élément personnel semble positif - il contourne le gouvernement et évite les grandes entreprises. Cependant, il contourne également l'impératif démocratique du gouvernement représentatif et réduit le développement à des actes d'aumône, le plus souvent visant à contourner les situations des sociétés rurales pauvres. Le cynisme à l'égard du volontariat est certainement mal placé. Le volontariat peut impliquer seulement une charité simple et louable. Toutefois, lorsque le tourisme de volontariat est présenté comme un développement durable et que la publicité des entreprises de vacances d'un an fusionne dans la pensée du développement, cela est symptomatique d'une dégradation du discours du développement. La politique du tourisme de volontariat représente un recul par rapport à une compréhension sociale des inégalités mondiales et de la pauvreté vécue par tant de personnes dans le monde en développement.

Amateur Astronomy

Many things have changed in astronomy over the past half-century. Until about 30 years ago, there was a great shortage of charts and catalogues. Telescopic equipment was limited and there were few books on practical astronomy. Today, the range of off-the-shelf telescopes and equipment covers almost everything one could need. Electronic calculators and computers have revolutionised almanacs and chart production, and facilitated the analysis of observations and the publication of results.
All this must surely make this the golden age of amateur astronomy. Well, perhaps, but a great deal has been lost as well. Now one may have to travel 80 km to find a sky comparable to that found in urban areas 50 years ago. The daytime skies are now plagued by aircraft condensation trails which can persist for hours and often spread out to form amorphous clouds, making solar observations impossible and hampering night-time observation too.

Too Much Choice

Society is becoming ‘overchoiced’. There are too many things to do, too many options, too many opportunities. In the new economy, the desire for the new product, service or next big thing is an addiction, and technology simply accelerates the pace of change: the noise, the proliferation of new goods and services, offering more and more choice. No sooner has the new product emerged off this virtual production line than the next one is about to be launched. The head spins, the brain races, the fatigue sets in; the disconnection from life begins.
Choice is the mantra of the new economy, but more choice means more stress, less time and more complexity. Hence a new trend is afoot. The search is on for ‘simplexity’ - the simple things that give meaning in an increasingly complex world. But simplifying your life is not easy in an age of economic excess. There are more basic brands of detergent and breakfast cereals than we can ever need or want, more software upgrades, features and calling plans than we can keep track of.

McAndrews Hotel

Every summer we spend a fortnight in McAndrews Hotel in North Mayo, Ireland. It is a family tradition, instigated by my grandmother, and by now it has achieved a certain sacredness. Nothing is allowed to interfere with the ritual. We are of a kind, McAndrews clientele: old-fashioned, odd perhaps, some would say snobbish. I do not like the bad manners, the insolence of shop assistants which passes for egalitarianism in this present age; I resent chummy overtures from waiters who sometimes appear to restrain themselves with difficulty from slapping one on the back. I know most of my fellow-guests’ names - like me they have been coming here since they were children - yet can rest assured that when I meet any of them in any part of the hotel, I shall be spared all social intercourse apart from a civil word of greeting. Such respect for dignity and personal privacy is hard to come by in commercial establishments these days.

Amateurastronomie

In de afgelopen vijftig jaar is er veel veranderd in de astronomie. Tot ongeveer dertig jaar geleden was er een groot tekort aan kaarten en catalogi. Telescoopapparatuur was beperkt en er waren weinig boeken over praktische astronomie. Tegenwoordig is de keuze aan telescopen en apparatuur bijna oneindig. Elektronische rekenmachines en computers hebben de almanakken en kaartproductie geëvolueerd en de analyse van waarnemingen en de publicatie van resultaten vergemakkelijkt.
Alles moet zeker de gouden eeuw van de amateurastronomie zijn. Misschien wel, maar er is ook veel verloren gegaan. Nu moet je misschien wel 80 km reizen om een hemel te vinden die vergelijkbaar is met die van stedelijke gebieden 50 jaar geleden. Overdag worden de luchten nu verpest door condensatietrajecten van vliegtuigen die urenlang kunnen aanhouden en vaak uitgroeien tot amorf wolken, waardoor zonneobservaties onmogelijk worden en ook nachtelijke observaties worden belemmerd.

Het nieuwe product is niet eens uit de virtuele productielijn voordat het volgende alweer wordt gelanceerd. Het hoofd draait rond, de hersenen racen, de vermoeidheid neemt toe; de ontkoppeling van het leven begint. Keuze is het mantra van de nieuwe economie, maar meer keuze betekent meer stress, minder tijd en meer complexiteit. Daarom is er een nieuwe trend in aantocht. Het is de zoektocht naar'simplexiteit' - de eenvoudige dingen die betekenis geven in een steeds complexere wereld. Maar het vereenvoudigen van je leven is niet gemakkelijk in een tijd van economische overdaad. Er zijn meer basismerken van wasmiddel en ontbijtgranen dan we ooit nodig of willen hebben, meer software-upgrades, functies en beltegoed dan we kunnen bijhouden.

Beaucoup de choses ont changé en astronomie au cours des cinquante dernières années. Jusqu'à il y a environ trente ans, il y avait un grand manque de cartes et de catalogues. L'équipement télescopique était limité et il y avait peu de livres sur l'astronomie pratique. Aujourd'hui, la gamme d'équipements et de télescopes prêts à l'emploi couvre presque tout ce dont on peut avoir besoin. Les calculatrices électroniques et les ordinateurs ont révolutionné les almanachs et la production de cartes, et ont facilité l'analyse des observations et la publication des résultats. Tout cela doit certainement faire de l'astronomie amateur l'âge d'or. Eh bien, peut-être, mais beaucoup a été perdu aussi. Aujourd'hui, il faut parcourir 80 km pour trouver un ciel comparable à celui des zones urbaines il y a 50 ans. Le ciel de jour est désormais infesté de traînées de condensation des avions, qui peuvent persister pendant des heures et s'étendre pour former des nuages amorphes, rendant les observations solaires impossibles et gênant les observations nocturnes aussi.

The Eden Project 

Since it opened, the Eden Project in the south-west of England has become one of the UK’s most popular tourist attractions. At first sight, the huge ‘biospheres’ on this former industrial site look like a scene from a science-fiction movie. 

Each biosphere contains a different climate zone, showing visitors just how important the relationship between people and plants is. It is amazing to see just how many products that we use every day come from plants: wood, rubber, fruit, rice, sugar, coffee and chocolate, for example. Over 135,000 different types of plant are grown here. However cold the weather is outside, computer-controlled electric heaters keep the plants at the right temperature. 
In the Rainforest Zone, the atmosphere is always damp because of a huge waterfall. Another zone reproduces the environment of the Mediterranean, California and South Africa, and there are plans to build a desert zone in the near future.

Het is verbazingwekkend om te zien hoeveel producten die we dagelijks gebruiken afkomstig zijn van planten: hout, rubber, fruit, rijst, suiker, koffie en chocolade, bijvoorbeeld. In de Rainforest Zone is de atmosfeer altijd vochtig vanwege een enorme waterval. Henry was acutely aware of the importance of securing a male heir during his reign. He was worried that he had only one surviving child, Mary, to show for his marriage to Catherine, who was now in her 40s. So the king asked Cardinal Wolsey to appeal to Pope Clement VII for an annulment and it soon became clear he wanted to marry Anne Boleyn, who had been a lady-in-waiting to his first wife.
But, unwilling to anger Catherine of Aragon's nephew – the most powerful ruler in Europe, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V – the Pope refused. Thomas Wolsey's ascendancy was cut short by this failure.
In 1533, Henry VIII broke with the church and married the now pregnant Anne Boleyn in a secret ceremony. Henry was excommunicated by the Pope. The English reformation had begun.
After Wolsey's downfall, Thomas Cromwell became Henry's chief minister and earned the confidence of the King by helping him to break with Rome and establish Henry VIII as head of the Church of England. This act also brought him much needed wealth through the dissolution of the well-funded monasteries. Over four years Cromwell ordered that 800 monasteries be disbanded and their lands and treasures taken for the crown.
The cultural and social impact was significant, as much of the land was sold to the gentry and churches and monasteries were gutted and destroyed. Henry's personal religious beliefs remained Catholic, despite the growing number of people at court and in the nation who had adopted Protestantism.

He had said exactly the name Emma wanted him to say. Now she could suggest that it was difficult to explain matters by letter, and she offered to go over to Rouen and speak to him directly. Charles would not hear of troubling her. She insisted. It was a battle of kindness. Finally, she cried, 'Now, not another word, please! I am going!'
'How kind you are!' he said, kissing her on the forehead.
The next morning she was off to Rouen in the coach, to consult Monsieur Leon. She stayed for three days. They were three wonderful days. They stayed down near the harbour at the Hotel de Boulogne, and there they lived, with the curtains closed, the doors locked, the floor covered with flowers, and iced drinks brought up every morning. Towards evening they would take a boat and go and have dinner on one of the islands. As they left the town, smoke rose up among the trees, and the red sun, reflected on the oily water of the harbour, looked like blood on polished metal. 
They went down between the rows of boats, and the noises of the town grew fainter and fainter. When, finally, they arrived at their favourite restaurant, she untied her hat and they stepped out of the boat on to their island. They went into a small cafe, with dark fishing-nets hung up at the door, and sat themselves down in the low-ceilinged room. They ate small fried fish, followed by cherries and cream, and then went and sat on the grass.

Schnauzer Dogs

There are three sizes of Schnauzer dog.
The two smaller sizes first came to England over 50 years ago, but the Giant Schnauzer has not been here very long. The name Giant is a good one because the dogs are 65 to 67.5 cm high.
All the dogs have long hair, which should be cut quite often. Most smaller Schnauzers are grey in colour, but the Giant Schnauzer is usually black.
Schnauzers come from Germany, where farmers use the dogs to help them with their sheep, and they are also used by the police, because Schnauzer dogs are very intelligent.
A Schnauzer makes a nice family dog. It is friendly and very good with young children.

Buffy knew that she was winning. 'Come on, Giles!'

'OK, OK!' Giles said quickly. 'That's enough for today. Go to your dance.'

Science flying in the face of gravity

Journalist Tom Mumford joins students using weightlessness to test their theories.

It looked like just another aircraft from the outside. The pilot told his young passengers that it was built in 1964, a Boeing KC-135 refuelling tanker, based on the Boeing 707 passenger craft.
But appearances were deceptive and the 13 students from Europe and America who boarded were in for the flight of their lives. Inside, it had become a long white tunnel.
There were almost no windows, but it was eerily illuminated by lights along the padded walls. Most of the seats had been ripped out, apart from a few at the back, where the pale-faced, budding scientists took their places with the air of condemned men.
For 12 months, they had competed with other students from across the continent to participate in the flight. The challenge, offered by the European Space Agency, had been to suggest imaginative experiments to be conducted in weightless conditions.
Those with the best ideas won a place on this unusual flight, which is best described as the most extraordinary roller-coaster ride yet devised. For the next two hours the Boeing's flight would resemble that of an enormous bird which had lost its reason, shooting upwards towards the heavens before hurtling towards Earth.
The intention was to achieve a kind of state of grace at the top of each curve. As the pilot cuts the engines at 3,000 metres, the aircraft throws itself still higher by virtue of its own momentum before gravity takes over and it plummets earthwards again.
In the few silent seconds between ascending and falling, the aircraft and everything inside it become weightless, and the 13 students would, in theory, feel themselves closer to the moon than the Earth. The aircraft took off smoothly enough, but any lingering illusions the young scientists and I had that we were on anything like a scheduled passenger service were quickly dispelled when the pilot put the Boeing into a 45-degree climb which lasted around 20 seconds. The engines strained wildly, blood drained from our heads, and bodies were scattered across the cabin floor.
Then the engines cut out and the transition to weightlessness was nearly instantaneous. For 20 seconds we conducted a ghostly dance in the unreal silence:the floor had become a vast trampoline, and one footstep was enough to launch us headlong towards the ceiling.
We floated aimlessly; the idea of going anywhere was itself confusing. Left or right, up or down, no longer had any meaning. Only gravity, by rooting us somewhere, permits us to appreciate the possibility of going somewhere else.
After ten seconds of freefall descent, the pilot pulled the aircraft out of its nose dive. The return of gravity was less immediate than its loss, but was still sudden enough to ensure that some of the students came down with a bump.
Our first curve completed, there were those who turned green at the thought of the 29 to follow. Thirty curves added up to ten minutes 'space time’ for experiments and the Dutch students were soon studying the movements of Leonardo, their robotic cat, hoping to discover how it is that cats always land on their feet.
At the appropriate moment the device they had built to investigate this was released, floating belly-up, and one of the students succeeded in turning it belly-down with radio-controlled movements. The next curve was nearly its last, however, when another student landed on top of it during a less well managed return to gravitational pull.
Next to the slightly stunned acrobatic robocat, a German team from the University of Aachen investigated how the quality of joins in metal is affected by the absence of gravity, with an eye to the construction of tomorrow's space stations.
Another team of students, from Utah State University, examined the possibility of creating solar sails from thin liquid films hardened in ultra-violet sunlight. Their flight was spent attempting to produce the films under microgravity. They believe that once the process is perfected, satellites could be equipped with solar sails that use the sun's radiation just as a yacht's sails use the wind. 
After two hours spent swinging between heaven and Earth, that morning’s breakfast felt unstable, but the predominant sensation was exhilaration, not nausea.
This was a feeling that would stay with us for a long time. ‘It was an unforgettable experience,’ said one of the students. 'I was already aiming to become an astronaut, but now I want to even more.’

Journalist Tom Mumford gaat met studenten mee die de zwaartekracht gebruiken om hun theorieën te testen.

Het leek op een ander vliegtuig van buiten. De piloot vertelde zijn jonge passagiers dat het een tanker was die in 1964 was gebouwd, gebaseerd op het passagiersvliegtuig Boeing 707. Maar het uiterlijk was bedrieglijk en de 13 studenten uit Europa en Amerika die aan boord gingen, waren klaar voor de vlucht van hun leven. Binnen was het een lange witte tunnel. Er waren bijna geen ramen, maar het was spookachtig verlicht door lampen langs de gewatteerde wanden. De meeste stoelen waren verwijderd, behalve een paar aan de achterkant, waar de bleke, opkomende wetenschappers plaats namen met de lucht van veroordeelde mannen.

Voor 12 maanden hadden de 13 studenten met andere studenten vanuit het hele continent meegedaan aan de wedstrijd om een ​​verbeeldingskrachtige experiment voor te stellen om uit te voeren in omstandigheden zonder zwaartekracht. Degenen met de beste ideeën wonnen een plekje op deze ongewone vlucht, die het beste kan worden beschreven als de meest buitengewone achtbaan rit die ooit is bedacht. Voor de volgende twee uur zou de vlucht van het vliegtuig lijken op die van een enorme vogel die zijn verstand heeft verloren, die omhoog schiet richting de hemel voordat hij naar de aarde toestormt.

Het doel was om een ​​soort staat van genade te bereiken op de top van elke bocht. Terwijl de piloot de motoren uitschakelt op 3.000 meter, gooit het vliegtuig zichzelf nog hoger door zijn eigen momentum voordat de zwaartekracht weer overneemt en het vliegtuig naar de aarde stort.

In de paar stille seconden tussen stijgen en vallen, wordt het vliegtuig en alles erin gewichtloos en zouden de jonge wetenschappers en ik ons in theorie dichter bij de maan dan de aarde voelen. Het vliegtuig vertrok soepel genoeg, maar elke illusie dat de jonge wetenschappers en ik hadden dat we op iets gelijkaardigs aan een geplande passagiersdienst zaten, werd snel verdrongen toen de piloot het vliegtuig in een 45-graden stijging bracht die ongeveer 20 seconden duurde. We dwaalden zonder doel; het idee om ergens naartoe te gaan was zelf verwarrend. Links of rechts, omhoog of omlaag, had geen betekenis meer. Alleen de zwaartekracht, door ons ergens te verankeren, laat ons de mogelijkheid zien om ergens anders naartoe te gaan.

He started walking down to the village. It was difficult because he was very tired. He went carefully because he didn't want to fall again. By the end of the day he was at the river, and he stopped for a drink. 
There were beautiful flowers near the river. 'This is a lovely place,' Nunez thought. There were a lot of small houses in the centre of the village. They looked very strange to him, because they didn't have any windows. 
He could see men and women at work in the village. Some were in the fields with their children. He could see gardens near the houses and there were fine vegetables in them. When Nunez was near the village, he shouted to some men. 
'Hello!' he shouted. 'Hello ... hello!' and he waved his arms. The men heard him and they turned their heads. They looked one way, and then the other way. They looked past Nunez, but they didn't look at him. 'Why can't they see me?' he thought. 
Nunez moved nearer and shouted again. He was now quite near three men. He waved again, but they didn't wave back to him. 'What's wrong with them?' he thought. 'Are they blind?' He walked down to the men, and then he saw their faces. 
He was right - the men were all blind. They had no eyes. 'Who is this?' one man asked his friend. 'A man? Or is it a spirit?' 'It's a man,' said the second man. 'I think it's a man.'

results.src_text:
Life was getting out of hand

Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual labour.

Everyone is in love with technology. It gives us all those marvellous gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology rules, and that it is OK.
These implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses nothing from the previous power supply being eaten up by our greedy race. A craft executed by hand does not pollute the environment.
However, a recent unhappy experience with my malfunctioning word processor -
a £48 call-out fee, a labour charge of £15 per quarter of an hour, plus parts and replacements costs - has confirmed a suspicion that gadgets are often not worth the expense or the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we imagine? Bit by bit, I have been letting the household technology fall by the wayside as its natural and often short life expires.
This makes me wonder just what 'time' technology gives us. The time to take up more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they are conning us.
So when the thing started making curious noises, which continued even when it was disconnected by a puzzled service agent, I abandoned it to the backyard, where it whispers damply to itself like some robot ghost.
I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, with my head bent and my back turned on the world, and I can take my time over the garment. In any case, I was always slightly alarmed by those electric machines that dash across the fabric towards your fingers. Best of all, I can pop the whole lot into a carrier bag and take it with me wherever I go.
Of course, there are some gadgets I would not like to be without. A year living without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose loss has brought unexpected delight. Feeling that we were becoming too apt to collapse in front of the television, or slot in a video, I sent back the rented colour equipment and we returned to the small black-and-white portable.
It is a real strain on the eyes and concentrates the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend a lot more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, talking or pursuing other hobbies.
One of these, in my own case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that went by the board. My old Singer sewing machine is now an ornamental plant table, and as l cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.
We have come to believe that we could not do without it, and if we do resist the notion that our lives would be unmanageable without the appliances of science we certainly do not want to relinquish them. Pity the generations whose lives were blighted by tedious and blister inducing toil. Even our brains are relieved of exertion by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed but now provide entertainment.
In fact, the time I now spend placidly stitching is anything but tedious, and the advantages are numerous. For a start, I can sew and listen to the radio - another rediscovered pleasure - or I can talk with family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programmes I do want to see on television, and alleviate my puritanical guilt at sitting in front of the box by doing something useful at the same time. And what a lovely, cosy feeling it is to sit by the fire and sew with a pot of tea for company.
Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of the women who sewed elaborate garments, robes, linen and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the strain on the eyes and so on. 
There is a wonderfully soothing quality about executing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction in watching one's work become neater, more assured. I find things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows down to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th century life the need to rush to finish an activity so that I can rush to the next.
Meanwhile I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and daydream while doing the washing up agreeable, if temporarily forgotten, activity.
The result of all this brooding is that I now prowl the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that powered lawnmower? Come to think of it, we could save an awful lot of money by doing without electric lights!

Maar een recente onaangename ervaring met mijn defecte tekstverwerker - een oproepkosten van £ 48, een arbeidskost van £ 15 per kwartier, plus onderdelen en vervangingen - heeft een vermoeden bevestigd dat gadgets vaak niet de moeite of de moeite waard zijn. Zijn we zo afhankelijk van technologie als we ons voorstellen? Beetje bij beetje heb ik de huishoudelijke technologie laten vallen naarmate de natuurlijke en vaak korte levensduur ervan verstrijkt.
Dit doet me afvragen wat 'tijd' technologie ons geeft. De tijd om meer activiteiten te ondernemen waarvoor we meer gadgets moeten kopen? Als dat zo is, hats off aan de marketingexperts: maar ik denk dat ze ons bedriegen.
Toen de ding vreemde geluiden begon te maken, die bleven zelfs toen het werd uitgeschakeld door een verbaasde serviceagent, heb ik het aan de achterkant van de tuin gezet, waar het zachtjes tegen zichzelf fluistert als een robotgeest.
Ik ben niet gebonden aan een rumoerige, ronkende machine, met mijn hoofd gebogen en mijn rug naar de wereld, en ik kan mijn tijd nemen over het kledingstuk. Bovendien was ik altijd een beetje bezorgd over die elektrische machines die naar je vingers snellen. Het beste van alles, ik kan alles in een draagtas stoppen en het overal mee naartoe nemen waar ik ga.
Natuurlijk zijn er gadgets waar ik niet zonder kan. Een jaar zonder wasmachine heeft me overtuigd van de waarde van de elektrische wasbak. Maar er zijn anderen wier verlies onverwachte vreugde heeft gebracht. Het idee dat we te gevoelig zijn om voor de televisie of een video te vallen, heb ik teruggebracht naar de huur van de kleurenapparatuur en we zijn teruggekeerd naar de kleine zwarte-witte draagbare.
Het is een echte belasting op de ogen en concentreert de geest op wat echt de moeite waard is om te kijken. We brengen nu veel meer tijd door met het wandelen van de hond (die de televisie toch nooit leuk vond), lezen, praten of andere hobby's beoefenen.
Een van deze hobby's, in mijn geval, is naaien; en hier is een ander gadget dat is afgevoerd. Mijn oude naaimachine van Singer is nu een plantenbaktafel, en omdat ik deze niet kan vervangen, doe ik het nu met handmatig naaien.
We zijn ertoe overgegaan te geloven dat we niet zonder de apparaten van de wetenschap konden leven, en als we ons daartegen verzetten, willen we ze zeker niet opgeven. Jammer voor de generaties wier leven werd geteisterd door vervelend en blaren veroorzakende arbeid. Zelfs onze hersenen worden bevrijd van inspanning door computers die niet alleen wonderbaarlijke berekeningen met verbazingwekkende snelheid uitvoeren, maar nu ook entertainment bieden.
In feite is het tijd dat ik nu rustig naai, allesbehalve vervelend, en de voordelen zijn talrijk. Om te beginnen kan ik naaien en naar de radio luisteren - een ander herontdekt plezier - of kan ik met familie en vrienden praten. Als het een eenvoudige taak is, kan ik de programma's kijken die ik wel wil zien op televisie, en verlicht mijn puriteinse geweten dat ik voor de televisie zit terwijl ik tegelijkertijd iets nuttigs doe. En wat een heerlijk, gezellig gevoel om bij het vuur te zitten en te naaien met een potje thee als gezelschap.
Niet alleen had ik met angst en beven gedacht aan de vrouwen die uitgebreide kledingstukken, gewaden, linnen en huishoudelijke artikelen met de hand maakten. Ik dacht aan al die lange uren, de spanning op de ogen enzovoort.
Er is een wonderbaarlijk rustgevend gevoel bij het uitvoeren van een ambacht met de hand, een grote voldoening in het zien van je werk mooier en zekerder worden. Ik merk dat dingen verrassend snel worden gedaan, en het tempo van het leven neemt plotseling de ritme van mijn eigen handen aan. Ik ben ook bevrijd van een van de meest verafschuwde aspecten van het late 20e-eeuwse leven de noodzaak om haast te maken om een activiteit af te maken, zodat ik haast kan maken naar de volgende.
Ondertussen loop ik door het huis met een speurend oog. Hebben we echt de behoefte aan de diepvriezer, de magnetron, die aangedreven grasmaaier? Komt het erop neer dat we veel geld kunnen besparen door zonder elektrische verlichting!

Ainsi, lorsque l'appareil a commencé à faire des bruits curieux, qui continuaient même lorsque l'appareil était débranché par un agent de service perplexe, j'ai abandonné l'appareil au fond du jardin, où il murmure doucement à lui-même comme un robot fantôme. Je ne suis pas lié à une machine bruyante, la tête penchée et le dos tourné sur le monde, et je peux prendre mon temps sur l'objet. De toute façon, j'ai toujours été légèrement inquiet par ces machines électriques qui se précipitent sur le tissu vers vos doigts. Mieux encore, je peux mettre tout dans un sac de transport et le prendre avec moi partout où je vais. Bien sûr, il y a des gadgets que je ne voudrais pas être sans. Une année de vie sans lave-linge m'a convaincu de la valeur de la cuve électrique. Mais il y a d'autres pertes dont l'absence a apporté un plaisir inattendu. Sentant que nous devenions trop enclins à s'effondrer devant la télévision ou à insérer une vidéo, j'ai renvoyé l'équipement en location couleur et nous avons retourné le petit appareil portable noir et blanc. C'est une vraie contrainte pour les yeux et concentre l'esprit sur ce qui vaut vraiment la peine d'être regardé. Mon vieux machine à coudre Singer est maintenant une plante en pot de table, et comme je ne peux pas me permettre de le remplacer, j'ai repris la couture à la main. Nous avons tendance à croire que nous ne pourrions pas nous passer des appareils de la science, et si nous résistons à l'idée que nos vies seraient désordonnées sans les appareils, nous ne voulons certainement pas les renoncer. Pitié pour les générations dont la vie a été gâchée par un travail ennuyeux et indolore. Même nos cerveaux sont soulagés de l'effort par des ordinateurs qui non seulement effectuent des calculs miraculeux avec une vitesse étonnante, mais fournissent également du divertissement. En fait, le temps que je passe à coudre paisiblement est tout sauf ennuyeux, et les avantages sont nombreux. Si c'est une tâche simple, je peux regarder les programmes que je veux voir à la télévision et alléger ma culpabilité puritaine en faisant quelque chose d'utile en même temps. Il y a une qualité merveilleusement apaisante à exécuter un artisanat à la main, une grande satisfaction à regarder son travail devenir plus soigné, plus assuré. French: Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual work. Everyone is in love with technology. It offers us all these wonderful gadgets that make life easier and leave us much more time to do other things. A great, albeit not very subtle, conditioning process has convinced us that technology is the rule and it is fine. The implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers does not require the previous power source that is consumed by our avid race. A job performed by hand does not pollute the environment. However, a recent unfortunate experience with my word processor - repair costs of £48, labor costs of £15 per hour, as well as parts and replacement costs - confirmed the suspicion that gadgets are not worth the money, nor the time, nor the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we think we are? Little by little, I have let go of household technologies as their natural and often short life fades away. It makes me wonder just how much time technology gives us. The time to take on more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, thanks to the marketing experts: but I think they are deceiving us. So, when the machine began to make strange noises, which continued even when the machine was unplugged by a perplexed service agent, I abandoned the machine at the bottom of the garden, where it whispers softly to itself like a ghost robot. I am not tied to a noisy machine, leaning my head and turning my back on the world, and I can take my time on the object. Anyway, I have always been slightly worried by these electric machines that rush towards your fingers on the fabric. Better yet, I can put everything in a carrying bag and take it with me everywhere I go. Of course, there are gadgets that I would not want to be without. A year of life without a washing machine has convinced me of the value of the electric drum. But there are other losses whose absence has brought unexpected pleasure. Feeling that we have become too inclined to collapse in front of the television or to insert a video, I returned the color rental equipment and we returned the small portable black and white machine. It is a real strain on the eyes and focuses the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend much more time walking the dog (who has never liked television anyway), reading, talking or practicing other hobbies. One of these hobbies, in my case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that has been put aside. My old Singer sewing machine is now a table plant pot, and since I cannot afford to replace it, I have taken up sewing by hand. We tend to believe that we could not do without the devices of science, and if we resist the idea that our lives would be disordered without the devices, we certainly do not want to give them up. Pity for the generations whose lives have been spoiled by boring and painless work. Even our brains are relieved of the effort by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed, but also provide entertainment. In fact, the time I spend peacefully sewing is anything but boring, and the benefits are many. To begin with, I can sew and listen to the radio - another pleasure rediscovered - or I can talk with my family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programs I want to see on television and lighten my puritanical guilt by doing something useful at the same time. And what a pleasant and comfortable feeling to be able to sit near the fireplace and sew with a cup of tea for company. Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of women who sewed elaborate clothes, dresses, linen items and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the eye strain and so on. There is a wonderfully soothing quality to performing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction to watch one's work become more skilled, more assured. I find that things are done surprisingly quickly, and life's pace suddenly stops at the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of the end of the 20th century: the need to rush to complete an activity in order to be able to rush towards the next. Meanwhile, I have regained control of my sink, where I dip my hands into the splashes and dream while doing the dishes. The result of all these reflections is that I walk around the house with a critical eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, the electric lawnmower? Think about it, we could save a huge amount of money by not relying on electric lamps!

Humphrey Partridge stood by the open door of the second bedroom. There was a smile on his lips as he looked at the empty bed.
'It's all right, Mother. Just the post,' Humphrey Partridge called from the bottom of the stairs, as he opened the door to the village postman.
'There's a package for you, Mr Partridge,' said Reg Carter, putting his hand on the door. 'From a garden centre, it says on it. Roses, I think.'
'Yes,' said Partridge, trying to close the door.
'It's the right time of year for planting roses, is it? November?'
'Yes.'
'How's your mother?' Reg went on. He was in no hurry to leave.
'Not so bad.'
'She never seems to get any letters, does she?'
'No. Well, when you reach that age, most of your friends are dead.'
'How old is she now?'
'She was eighty-six last July.'
'That's a good age. She doesn't go out much, does she?'
'No, not at all. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to leave to catch my train to work.'
Partridge closed the door and called up the stairs, 'Goodbye, Mother. I'm off to work.'
On his way to the station he stopped at the village shop to get his newspaper.
'Good morning,' said Mr Denton, the shopkeeper. 'How's the old lady?'
'Oh, not too bad, thank you - for her age, that is.'
'Oh, Mr Partridge,' said Mrs Denton, 'there's going to be a meeting in the village hall on Sunday, about-'
'I'm sorry, Mrs Denton, I don't like to leave my mother at weekends. I'm at work all week, you see.' He hurried away.

An awfully big adventure

The Taklamakan Desert in western China is one of the last unexplored places on earth. It is also one of the most dangerous. Charles Blackmore crossed it, and lived to tell the tale.

There are very few big adventures left and very few heroes. Children’s stories used to specialise in them — courageous explorers with sunburnt, leathery skin and eyes narrowed by straining to see into far horizons on their journeys into the unknown. These days you no longer find such people in fiction, let alone in real life. Or so I thought until I met Charles Blackmore.
Blackmore’s great adventure consisted of leading an expedition across one of the last unexplored places on earth, the Taklamakan Desert in western China. Its name means ‘once entered you never come out’, but local people call it the Desert of Death. He recalled the dangers and exhilaration of that amazing trek, in the calm atmosphere of his family home.
The team he led was composed of four Britons (one of them the party’s medical officer), an American photographer, four Chinese (all experts on the area), 30 camels and six camel handlers. It later turned out that the camel handlers had never worked with camels before, but were long-distance lorry drivers: a misunderstanding that could have cost everyone their lives and certainly jeopardised the expedition’s success. This mixed bunch set out to cross 1,200 kilometres of the world’s least hospitable desert and Charles Blackmore has written a mesmerising account of their journey. 
At the time, he was about to leave the Army after 14 happy years. He launched the expedition for fun, to fill a gap in his life, to prove something. ‘I had always assumed I’d spend my whole life in the Army. I had been offered promotion but suddenly I felt I wanted to see who Charles Blackmore really was, outside all that. It was a tremendous gamble. Tina, my wife, was very worried that I wouldn’t come back as nobody had ever done that route; we went into it blind. In the event, it took 59 days to cross from west to east, and the desert was very kind to us.’
Anyone reading his extraordinary account of that crossing will wonder at the use of the word ‘kind’. The team suffered unspeakable hardships: dysentery; extremes of temperature; severe thirst and dehydration; the loss of part of their precious water supply. ‘But’, Blackmore explains, ‘when we were at the limits of our own endurance and the camels had gone without water for seven days, we managed to find some. We didn’t experience the Taklamakan’s legendary sandstorms. And we never hit the raw, biting desert cold that would have totally immobilised us. That’s not to say that we weren’t fighting against hurdles the whole time. The fine sand got into everything, especially blisters and wounds. The high dunes were torture to climb, for us and for the heavily laden camels, which often rolled over onto us.
‘What drove me on more than anything else was the need to survive. We had no contingency plan. Neither our budget no time allowed one. No aircraft ever flew over us. Once we got into the sandhills we were completely on our own.
‘I knew I had the mental stamina for the trip but I was very scared of my physical ability to do it. I remember day one — we sat at the edge of the desert and it was such an inferno that you couldn’t breathe. I thought, “We’ve got to do it now!” At that moment I was a very scared man.’
If it was like that at the beginning, how did they feel towards the end? ‘When you’ve walked for 1,000 kilometres you’re not going to duck out. You’ve endured so much; you’ve got so much behind you. We were very thin, but very muscular and sinewy despite our physical exhaustion. My body was well-toned and my legs were like pistons. I could walk over anything.’
Midway through the book, Blackmore went on to describe lying in the desert gazing up at a full moon, thinking of his family. How conscious was he of the ordeal it must have been for them? ‘Inside me there’s someone trying to find peace with himself. When I have doubts about myself now, I go back to the image of the desert and think, well, we managed to pull that together. As a personal achievements, I feel prouder of that expedition than of anything else I’ve dine. Yet in terms of a lifetime’s achievement, I think of my family and the happiness we share — against that yardstick, the desert does not measure up, does not compare.’
Has Charles Blackmore found peace? ‘I yearn for the challenge — for the open spaces — the resolve of it all. We were buoyed up by the sense of purpose. I find it difficult now to be part of the uniformity of modern life.’

Een enorme avontuur

De Taklamakanwoestijn in het westen van China is een van de laatste onontdekte plekken op aarde. Het is ook een van de gevaarlijkste. Charles Blackmore is erover gegaan en heeft het overleefd.

Er zijn maar weinig grote avonturen meer en er zijn maar weinig helden meer. In kinderverhalen waren het vroeger heldhaftige ontdekkingsreizigers met een bruin, lederen huid en ogen die nauwelijks konden zien vanwege de inspanning om ver in de verte te kijken. Tegenwoordig vind je dergelijke mensen niet meer in fictie, laat staan in het echte leven. Tot ik Charles Blackmore ontmoette.

Blackmores grote avontuur bestond erin een expeditie aan te voeren over een van de laatste onontdekte plekken op aarde, de Taklamakanwoestijn in het westen van China. Zijn naam betekent 'als je er eenmaal bent ingegaan, kom je nooit meer terug', maar de lokale bevolking noemt het de Doodswijde. Hij herinnerde zich de gevaren en de opwinding van die geweldige tocht, in de kalme sfeer van zijn gezinswoning.

Het team dat hij aanvoerde bestond uit vier Britten (waaronder de medisch officier van de partij), een Amerikaanse fotograaf, vier Chinezen (allen experts op het gebied) en 30 kamelen en zes kamelenhoeders. Later bleek dat de kamelenhoeders nog nooit met kamelen hadden gewerkt, maar langeafstandstruckers waren: een misverstand dat hun leven had kunnen kosten en het succes van de expeditie had kunnen schaden. Deze gemengde groep vertrok om 1.200 kilometer van's werelds minst gastvrije woestijn te oversteken en Charles Blackmore heeft een betoverend verslag geschreven van hun reis.

Op dat moment was hij op het punt om het leger te verlaten na 14 gelukkige jaren. Hij begon de expeditie voor de lol, om een leemte in zijn leven te vullen, om iets te bewijzen. 'Ik had altijd aangenomen dat ik mijn hele leven in het leger zou doorbrengen. Ik had een promotie aangeboden gekregen, maar opeens voelde ik dat ik iets van Charles Blackmore buiten al dat wilde zien. Het was een enorme gok. Tina, mijn vrouw, was erg bezorgd dat ik niet terug zou komen omdat niemand ooit die route had afgelegd; we gingen er blind in. Uiteindelijk duurde het 59 dagen om van west naar oost te gaan en de woestijn was erg vriendelijk voor ons.'

Iedereen die zijn buitengewone verslag van die oversteek leest zal zich afvragen waarom hij het woord 'vriendelijk' gebruikt. Het team leed onvoorstelbare ontberingen: dysenterie, extreme temperaturen, ernstige dorst en dehydratie, het verlies van een deel van hun kostbare watervoorraad. 'Maar', legt Blackmore uit, 'toen we aan de grenzen van onze eigen uithoudingsvermogen waren en de kamelen zeven dagen lang zonder water hadden gezeten, vonden we toch water. We hadden geen last van de legendarische zandstormen in de Taklamakan. En we hebben nooit de koude in de woestijn gehad die ons volledig zou hebben immobiliseerd. Dat wil niet zeggen dat we niet voortdurend tegen hindernissen aanliepen. Het fijne zand kwam in alles terecht, vooral in blaren en wonden. De hoge duinen waren een marteling voor ons en voor de zwaar beladen kamelen, die vaak over ons heen rolden.

'Wat mij het meeste dreef was de noodzaak te overleven. We hadden geen noodplan. Geen enkele luchtvaartmaatschappij vloog ooit over ons. Toen we in de zandheuvels terechtkwamen, waren we volledig op onszelf aangewezen.

'Ik wist dat ik de mentale uithoudingsvermogen had voor de reis, maar ik was erg bang voor mijn fysieke vermogen om het te doen. Ik herinner me dag één — we zaten aan de rand van de woestijn en het was zo'n hel dat je niet kon ademen. Ik dacht: 'We moeten het nu doen!' Op dat moment was ik een erg bange man.'

Als het zo was aan het begin, hoe voelden ze zich tegen het einde? 'Toen je 1.000 kilometer hebt gelopen, ben je niet van plan om op te geven. Je hebt zoveel verdragen; je hebt zoveel achter je. We waren erg dun, maar erg gespierd en gespierd ondanks onze fysieke uitputting. Mijn lichaam was goed getraind en mijn benen waren als zuigers. Ik kon over alles lopen.'

Halverwege het boek beschreef Blackmore hoe hij in de woestijn lag te kijken naar de volle maan, terwijl hij aan zijn familie dacht. Hoe bewust was hij van de orde die het moet hebben veroorzaakt voor hen? 'In mij zit iemand die op zoek is naar innerlijke vrede. Toen ik twijfel had over mezelf nu, ging ik terug naar de beelden van de woestijn en dacht: 'Nou, we hebben het samen kunnen doen. Als persoonlijke prestatie voel ik me trotser op die expeditie dan op alles wat ik ooit heb gedaan. Maar in termen van een levenslange prestatie, denk ik aan mijn familie en het geluk dat we samen delen — daar kan de woestijn niet tegen op.

An awfully big adventure

The Taklamakan Desert in western China is one of the last unexplored places on earth. It is also one of the most dangerous. Charles Blackmore crossed it, and lived to tell the tale.

There are very few big adventures left and very few heroes. Children’s stories used to specialise in them — courageous explorers with sunburnt, leathery skin and eyes narrowed by straining to see into far horizons on their journeys into the unknown. These days you no longer find such people in fiction, let alone in real life. Or so I thought until I met Charles Blackmore.
Blackmore’s great adventure consisted of leading an expedition across one of the last unexplored places on earth, the Taklamakan Desert in western China. Its name means ‘once entered you never come out’, but local people call it the Desert of Death. He recalled the dangers and exhilaration of that amazing trek, in the calm atmosphere of his family home.
The team he led was composed of four Britons (one of them the party’s medical officer), an American photographer, four Chinese (all experts on the area), 30 camels and six camel handlers. It later turned out that the camel handlers had never worked with camels before, but were long-distance lorry drivers: a misunderstanding that could have cost everyone their lives and certainly jeopardised the expedition’s success. This mixed bunch set out to cross 1,200 kilometres of the world’s least hospitable desert and Charles Blackmore has written a mesmerising account of their journey. 
At the time, he was about to leave the Army after 14 happy years. He launched the expedition for fun, to fill a gap in his life, to prove something. ‘I had always assumed I’d spend my whole life in the Army. I had been offered promotion but suddenly I felt I wanted to see who Charles Blackmore really was, outside all that. It was a tremendous gamble. Tina, my wife, was very worried that I wouldn’t come back as nobody had ever done that route; we went into it blind. In the event, it took 59 days to cross from west to east, and the desert was very kind to us.’
Anyone reading his extraordinary account of that crossing will wonder at the use of the word ‘kind’. The team suffered unspeakable hardships: dysentery; extremes of temperature; severe thirst and dehydration; the loss of part of their precious water supply. ‘But’, Blackmore explains, ‘when we were at the limits of our own endurance and the camels had gone without water for seven days, we managed to find some. We didn’t experience the Taklamakan’s legendary sandstorms. And we never hit the raw, biting desert cold that would have totally immobilised us. That’s not to say that we weren’t fighting against hurdles the whole time. The fine sand got into everything, especially blisters and wounds. The high dunes were torture to climb, for us and for the heavily laden camels, which often rolled over onto us.
‘What drove me on more than anything else was the need to survive. We had no contingency plan. Neither our budget no time allowed one. No aircraft ever flew over us. Once we got into the sandhills we were completely on our own.
‘I knew I had the mental stamina for the trip but I was very scared of my physical ability to do it. I remember day one — we sat at the edge of the desert and it was such an inferno that you couldn’t breathe. I thought, “We’ve got to do it now!” At that moment I was a very scared man.’
If it was like that at the beginning, how did they feel towards the end? ‘When you’ve walked for 1,000 kilometres you’re not going to duck out. You’ve endured so much; you’ve got so much behind you. We were very thin, but very muscular and sinewy despite our physical exhaustion. My body was well-toned and my legs were like pistons. I could walk over anything.’
Midway through the book, Blackmore went on to describe lying in the desert gazing up at a full moon, thinking of his family. How conscious was he of the ordeal it must have been for them? ‘Inside me there’s someone trying to find peace with himself. When I have doubts about myself now, I go back to the image of the desert and think, well, we managed to pull that together. As a personal achievements, I feel prouder of that expedition than of anything else I’ve dine. Yet in terms of a lifetime’s achievement, I think of my family and the happiness we share — against that yardstick, the desert does not measure up, does not compare.’
Has Charles Blackmore found peace? ‘I yearn for the challenge — for the open spaces — the resolve of it all. We were buoyed up by the sense of purpose. I find it difficult now to be part of the uniformity of modern life.’

L'aventure incroyablement grande

Le désert du Taklamakan, dans l'ouest de la Chine, est l'un des derniers endroits inexplorés de la terre. C'est aussi l'un des plus dangereux. Charles Blackmore l'a traversé, et il a vécu pour le raconter.

Il n'y a plus beaucoup d'aventures grandioses et de héros. Les contes pour enfants spécialisaient autrefois dans les explorateurs courageux aux peaux brûlées par le soleil et aux yeux rétrécis par l'effort de voir au loin sur leurs voyages dans l'inconnu. De nos jours, on ne trouve plus de tels gens dans la fiction, sans parler de la vie réelle. Ou du moins, c'est ce que je pensais jusqu'à ce que je rencontre Charles Blackmore.

L'aventure extraordinaire de Blackmore a consisté à diriger une expédition à travers l'un des derniers endroits inexplorés de la terre, le désert du Taklamakan dans l'ouest de la Chine. Son nom signifie « une fois entré, on ne peut plus sortir », mais les gens du pays l'appellent le désert de la mort. Il a raconté les dangers et l'exaltation de cette incroyable traversée, dans l'atmosphère calme de la maison de sa famille.

L'équipe qu'il a dirigée était composée de quatre Britanniques (dont l'un était le médecin de la partie), un photographe américain, quatre Chinois (tous experts de la région), 30 chameaux et six gardes-chameaux. Il s'est ensuite avéré que les gardes-chameaux n'avaient jamais travaillé avec des chameaux auparavant, mais étaient des chauffeurs de poids lourds longue distance : une erreur qui aurait pu coûter la vie à tout le monde et certainement compromis la réussite de l'expédition. Ce groupe hétéroclite a entrepris de traverser 1 200 kilomètres du désert le moins hospitalier de la terre et Charles Blackmore a écrit un récit envoûtant de leur voyage.

À l'époque, il était sur le point de quitter l'armée après 14 années de bonheur. Il a lancé l'expédition pour s'amuser, pour combler un vide dans sa vie, pour prouver quelque chose. « J'avais toujours supposé que je passerais toute ma vie dans l'armée. On m'avait offert une promotion, mais soudain, j'ai eu l'impression de vouloir voir qui était vraiment Charles Blackmore, en dehors de tout cela. C'était un pari énorme. Tina, ma femme, était très inquiète du fait que je ne reviendrais pas car personne n'avait jamais fait ce parcours ; nous y sommes allés à l'aveugle. En fait, il a fallu 59 jours pour traverser d'est en ouest, et le désert a été très gentil avec nous. »

Quiconque lisant son extraordinaire récit de ce passage se demandera à quel point on peut utiliser le mot « gentil ». L'équipe a subi des souffrances indescriptibles : la dysenterie, des extrêmes de température, une grave soif et déshydratation, la perte d'une partie de leur précieuse réserve d'eau. « Mais », explique Blackmore, « quand nous étions au bord de nos propres capacités et que les chameaux n'avaient pas bu d'eau pendant sept jours, nous avons réussi à en trouver. Nous n'avons pas connu les légendaires tempêtes de sable du Taklamakan. Et nous n'avons jamais été confrontés au froid brutal du désert qui aurait totalement immobilisé nous. Cela ne veut pas dire que nous n'avons pas eu à affronter des obstacles tout le temps. La poussière fine est entrée partout, en particulier dans les boutons et les plaies. Les hautes dunes étaient une torture à gravir, pour nous et pour les chameaux lourdement chargés, qui ont souvent roulé sur nous.
« Ce qui m'a poussé au-delà de tout autre chose, c'était le besoin de survivre. Nous n'avions aucun plan de secours. Ni notre budget ni notre temps le permettaient. Aucun avion ne nous a jamais survolés. Une fois que nous sommes entrés dans les collines de sable, nous étions complètement seuls.
« Je savais que j'avais la force mentale pour le voyage, mais j'avais très peur de ma capacité physique à le faire. Je me souviens du premier jour - nous nous sommes assis au bord du désert et c'était tellement infernal que vous ne pouviez pas respirer. Je me suis dit : « Nous devons le faire maintenant! » À ce moment-là, j'étais un homme très effrayé. »
Si c'était comme ça au début, comment se sont-ils sentis à la fin? « Quand vous avez marché pendant 1 000 kilomètres, vous n'êtes pas prêts à reculer. Vous avez enduré tellement ; vous avez tout derrière vous. Nous étions très maigres, mais très musclés et sineurys malgré notre épuisement physique. Mon corps était bien tonique et mes jambes étaient comme des pistons. Je pouvais marcher sur n'importe quoi. »
À mi-parcours du livre, Blackmore a décrit se coucher dans le désert en contemplant la pleine lune, en pensant à sa famille. Comment était-il conscient de l'épreuve qu'il a dû subir pour elles? « À l'intérieur de moi, il y a quelqu'un qui essaie de trouver la paix avec soi-même. Quand j'ai des doutes à propos de moi-même maintenant, je me remémore l'image du désert et je pense : « Eh bien, nous avons réussi à le faire maintenant. En termes de réussite personnelle, je me sens plus fier de cette expédition que de tout ce que j'ai fait. Pourtant, en termes de réussite de toute une vie, je pense à ma famille et au bonheur que nous partageons - contre ce critère, le désert ne mesure pas, ne se compare pas. »
Charles Blackmore a-t-il trouvé la paix? « J'ai envie de la confrontation - pour les espaces ouverts - la résolution de tout cela. Nous avons été soutenus par le sentiment d'objectif. Je trouve difficile maintenant d'être partie intégrante de la uniformité de la vie moderne. »
