Keeping the holiday-makers happy

A chalet girl’s work is never done, Sarah Sutherland-Pilch tells Veronica Lee - in between making beds and delicious dinners. 

This is the second year as a chalet girl for Sarah Sutherland-Pilch, a 24-year-old from West Sussex. Known by her nickname, Pilch, Sarah works for a company in Val d’Isere, France, cooking and cleaning for visitors who come to ski and stay in the wooden houses, known as chalets, that are characteristic of the area. Sarah graduated in French and History of Art from Oxford Brookes University last summer. 
Being a chalet girl isn't a career, she says, but an enjoyable way to spend a year or two before settling down. 'It's a good way to make contacts. I meet successful people every week.' 
Sarah does not 'live in'. She gets up at 7a.m. to walk the mile or so to the chalet, which sleeps up to 18 guests each week. She has her own breakfast before preparing that of the guests. 'They get the works - porridge, eggs, cereals, fruit and croissants.' When the last of the guests has had breakfast, by about 9.30 a.m., Sarah clears up and either makes the afternoon tea, which is left for the guests to help themselves, or cleans the rooms - 'the worst part of the job,' she says. 
By about 11 a.m. she is ready to go on the slopes herself. She skis as much as possible. ‘On a good day we can be up there until 4.30 p.m.' Sarah returns to the chalet in time to prepare dinner and takes a shower before doing so, but does not sleep. 'It's fatal if you do,' she says. 
Dinner, a three-course affair, is served at 8 p.m. and coffee is usually on the table by 10 p.m. Sarah clears away the dinner things and fills the dishwasher. 'There's nothing worse than coming in to a messy kitchen the next morning.' Sometimes she will stay and chat with the guests, other times they are content to be left alone. 'Good guests can make a week brilliant - breakfast this morning was great fun - but some weeks, for whatever reason, don't go quite so well.' 
Sarah meets her friends in the chalet where she lives - and they go out at about 11 p.m. 'We usually start off in Bananas, might go to G Jay’s and perhaps Dick’s T-Bar at the end of the evening,' she says. But Sarah never stays out too late on Saturday night as Sunday is her busiest time of the week. ‘A frightful day,' she says, 'when you certainly don't want to be cooking breakfast with a terrible headache.' 
Work begins earlier than usual on Sunday, since breakfast for guests who are leaving has to be on the table by 7 a.m. As soon as the guests are gone, Sarah starts cleaning madly. ’We just blitz the place - clear the breakfast, strip the beds, get everything ready.' If she hasn't already done the week's shop on Saturday, Sarah does it now. 
At around 3 p.m., the cleaning work done, Sarah then prepares tea for the new guests. 'They get here at around 4.30 p.m.' Sometimes they are disorientated and full of questions. I'm sure it's the mountain air that does something to them.' 
Between tea and dinner, Sarah takes any guests needing boots or skis down to the ski shop and then gets a lift back to the chalet from one of the ski shop staff. It is soon time for dinner duty again and perhaps a drink later, but not always. ’Sometimes I'm so tired I just have an early night,' she says.

De vakantiegangers blij maken
Het werk van een chaletmeisje is nooit af, vertelt Sarah Sutherland-Pilch tegen Veronica Lee - tussen het maken van bedden en heerlijke diners door. Dit is het tweede jaar dat Sarah Sutherland-Pilch, een 24-jarige uit West Sussex, werkt als chaletmeisje. Ze werkt voor een bedrijf in Val d'Isere, Frankrijk, en kookt en maakt schoon voor bezoekers die komen skiën en in de houten huizen, ook wel chalets genoemd, verblijven. Sarah studeerde Frans en Kunstgeschiedenis aan de Oxford Brookes University en is afgestudeerd in de zomer. Werken als chaletmeisje is geen carrière, zegt ze, maar een leuke manier om een jaar of twee door te brengen voordat ze zich vestigt. 'Het is een goede manier om contacten te leggen. Ik ontmoet succesvolle mensen elke week.' Sarah woont niet in het chalet. Ze staat op om 7 uur's ochtends om een mijl of zo naar het chalet te lopen, dat plaats biedt aan maximaal 18 gasten per week. Ze heeft haar eigen ontbijt voordat ze dat van de gasten voorbereidt. 'Ze krijgen het volledige ontbijt - ontbijtgranen, eieren, ontbijtgranen, fruit en croissants.' Rond 9.30 uur's ochtends is het laatste ontbijt klaar en maakt Sarah alles op orde. 'Het is het ergste deel van het werk,' zegt ze. Rond 11 uur is ze klaar om zelf de piste op te gaan. Ze skiet zoveel mogelijk. 'Op een goede dag kunnen we er tot 16.30 uur blijven.' Sarah keert terug naar het chalet op tijd om het diner voor te bereiden en neemt een douche voordat ze dat doet, maar ze slaapt niet. 'Het is fataal als je dat doet,' zegt ze. Het driegangendiner wordt om 20 uur geserveerd en koffie staat meestal om 22 uur op tafel. Sarah ruimt het diner op en vult de vaatwasser. 'Er is niets erger dan een keuken aan te treffen die een rommeltje is als je's ochtends komt.' Soms blijft ze en praat met de gasten, andere keren laten ze zich graag alleen. 'Goede gasten kunnen een week fantastisch maken - het ontbijt van vandaag was geweldig,' zegt ze. Sarah ontmoet haar vrienden in het chalet waar ze woont en ze gaan uit om ongeveer 23 uur. 'We beginnen meestal in Bananas, misschien naar G Jay's en aan het einde van de avond naar Dick's T-Bar,' zegt ze. Maar Sarah blijft nooit te laat op zaterdagavond, want zondag is haar drukste dag van de week. 'Een verschrikkelijke dag,' zegt ze, 'als je dan's ochtends met een verschrikkelijke hoofdpijn het ontbijt moet voorbereiden.' De werkdag begint vroeger dan gebruikelijk op zondag, want het ontbijt voor gasten die vertrekken moet op tafel staan om 7 uur. Zodra de gasten vertrokken zijn, begint Sarah te schoonmaken. 'We maken gewoon een blitz door het huis - het ontbijt opruimen, de bedden opmaken, alles klaarzetten.' Als ze het weekelijk boodschappen niet al op zaterdag heeft gedaan, doet ze dat nu. Rond 15 uur is het schoonmaakwerk gedaan en bereidt Sarah thee voor de nieuwe gasten. 'Ze komen rond 15.30 uur aan.' Soms zijn ze verward en vol vragen. 'Ik ben er zeker van dat de berglucht iets met ze doet,' zegt ze. Tussen het thee en het diner neemt Sarah eventuele gasten die skischoenen of ski's nodig hebben mee naar de skiwinkel en krijgt ze een lift terug naar het chalet van een van de medewerkers van de skiwinkel. Het is alweer tijd voor het diner en misschien een drankje later, maar niet altijd. 'Soms ben ik zo moe dat ik vroeg naar bed ga,' zegt ze.

Elle se lève à 7 heures du matin pour marcher un mile ou deux jusqu'au chalet, qui peut accueillir jusqu'à 18 invités chaque semaine. Elle prend son petit déjeuner avant de préparer celui des invités. «Ils ont le plein d'options - porridge, œufs, céréales, fruits et croissants.» Quand le dernier des invités a pris son petit déjeuner, vers 9h30, Sarah règle les choses et soit prépare le thé de l'après-midi, qui est laissé pour les invités de se servir eux-mêmes, ou nettoie les chambres - «la partie la plus difficile du travail», dit-elle. Vers 11 heures, elle est prête à monter sur les pistes. Elle skie autant que possible. «Le bon jour, on peut être là-haut jusqu'à 16h30.» Sarah retourne au chalet à temps pour préparer le dîner et prend une douche avant de le faire, mais ne dort pas. «C'est fatal si vous le faites», dit-elle. Le dîner, un repas en trois services, est servi à 20 heures et le café est généralement sur la table vers 22 heures. Sarah enlève les restes du dîner et remplit la machine à laver la vaisselle. «Il n'y a rien de pire que de venir dans une cuisine sale le lendemain matin.» Parfois, elle reste et discute avec les invités, d'autres fois ils sont contents de rester seuls. «Les bons invités peuvent rendre une semaine magnifique - le petit déjeuner ce matin était très amusant - mais certaines semaines, pour quelque raison que ce soit, ne vont pas si bien.» Sarah rencontre ses amis dans le chalet où elle vit - et ils sortent vers 23 heures. «Nous commençons généralement au Bananas, pouvons aller au G Jay's et finirons peut-être au Dick's T-Bar en fin de soirée», dit-elle. Mais Sarah ne reste jamais trop tard le samedi soir car le dimanche est sa journée la plus chargée de la semaine. «Une journée terrifiante», dit-elle, «quand vous ne voulez certainement pas être en train de préparer le petit déjeuner avec une terrible tête.» Le travail commence plus tôt que d'habitude le dimanche, car le petit déjeuner pour les invités qui partent doit être sur la table à 7 heures. Dès que les invités sont partis, Sarah commence à nettoyer follement. «Nous nettoyons simplement la place - ranger le petit déjeuner, enlever les draps, tout préparer.» Si elle n'a pas déjà fait les courses le samedi, Sarah le fait maintenant. Vers 15 heures, le nettoyage terminé, Sarah prépare le thé pour les nouveaux invités. «Ils arrivent vers 16h30.» Parfois, ils sont déorientés et pleins de questions. «Je suis sûre que c'est l'air de la montagne qui fait quelque chose à eux», dit-elle. Entre le thé et le dîner, Sarah emmène les invités ayant besoin de bottes ou de skis au magasin de ski et prend ensuite un trajet en voiture jusqu'au chalet avec l'un des membres du personnel du magasin. Il est bientôt temps de préparer le dîner de nouveau et peut-être un verre plus tard, mais pas toujours. «Parfois, je suis tellement fatiguée que je me couche tôt», dit-elle.
results.back_text: Cheer up holidaymakers Sarah Sutherland-Pilch tells Veronica Lee - between making the bed and cooking up delicious dinners. This is the second year as a chalet girl for Sarah Sutherland-Pilch, a 24-year-old from West Sussex. Known as Pilch, Sarah works for a company in Val d'Isere, France, cooking and cleaning for visitors who come to ski and stay in the wooden chalets, which are a feature of the area. Sarah graduated in French and art history from Brookes University, Oxford, last summer. Being a chalet girl is not a career, she says, but a nice way to spend a year or two before settling down. "It's a good way of making contacts. I meet prosperous people every week." Sarah does not "live" there. She gets up at 7am to walk a mile or two to the chalet, which can accommodate up to 18 guests each week. She has breakfast before preparing the guests'. "They have plenty of options - porridge, eggs, cereals, fruit and croissants." When the last guest has had breakfast, around 9.30am, Sarah tidies up and either makes afternoon tea, which is left for guests to help themselves, or cleans the bedrooms - "the hardest part of the job," she says. By 11am, she is ready to hit the slopes. She skis as much as possible. "On a good day, we can be up there until 4.30pm." Sarah is back at the chalet in time to prepare dinner and takes a shower before doing so, but does not sleep. "It's fatal if you do," she says. Dinner, a three-course meal, is served at 8pm and coffee is usually on the table by 10pm. Sarah removes the leftovers from dinner and fills the dishwasher. "There's nothing worse than coming into a dirty kitchen the next morning." Sometimes she stays and chats with guests, other times they are happy to be on their own. "Good guests can make a week wonderful - the breakfast this morning was great fun - but some weeks, for whatever reason, just don't go so well." Sarah meets her friends in the chalet where she lives - and they go out around 11pm. "We usually start at the Bananas, might go to G Jay's and end up at Dick's T-Bar later on," she says. But Sarah never stays out too late on a Saturday night because Sunday is her busiest day of the week. "A terrifying day," she says, "when you really don't want to be up preparing breakfast with a terrible head." Sunday work starts earlier than usual, as breakfast for departing guests must be on the table by 7am. As soon as the guests have gone, Sarah starts cleaning furiously. "We just tidy up - clear away breakfast, take down the bedding, get everything ready." If she hasn't already done the shopping on Saturday, Sarah does it now. By 3pm, the cleaning is done, Sarah prepares tea for new guests. "They arrive around 5.30pm." Sometimes they are disorientated and full of questions. "I'm sure it's the mountain air that does something to them," she says. Between tea and dinner, Sarah takes guests needing boots or skis to the ski shop and then takes a drive with one of the shop's staff members to the chalet. It's soon time to prepare dinner again and maybe a drink later, but not always. "Sometimes I'm so tired I go to bed early," she says.

Detective-Inspector Cornish and Chief-Inspector Craddock were discussing the murder at the local police station.
'Mrs Bantry said that Marina Gregg had a "frozen look"', said Cornish. 'Did she see someone on the stairs? There were two people from America - Ardwyck Fenn and Lola Brewster, a film star. There was a girl from London with a camera, but she had been there for half an hour already.'
'The strangers from the United States are our chief suspects,' said Craddock. 'Ardwyck Fenn was an old boyfriend of Marina's. Lola Brewster was married to Marina Gregg's third husband. He divorced her to marry Marina.'
'So perhaps Lola Brewster tried to kill Marina,' said Cornish. 'But the divorce was fifteen years ago. Miss Brewster has married twice again since then. I think I'll go to London and talk to Ardwyck Fenn, Lola Brewster and the photographer girl - what's her name? - Margot Bence. But perhaps it was the butler, Giuseppe. He was busy with the drinks and glasses.'
'Giuseppe?' asked Cornish. 'Do you think he's a suspect?'
'I don't think so,' said Craddock, 'but he might have a reason for killing Marina. And there are other people who were near the glasses. The secretary woman, Ella Zielinsky, for example. Nobody was interested in watching her.'
The phone rang. Cornish picked it up, listened for a moment, then put it down and looked at Craddock. 'Miss Marina Gregg,' he said, 'is feeling better. She's ready to be interviewed.'

Vervet monkeys

Cheney and Seyfarth describe how one day the dominant male in the group of vervet monkeys they were studying noticed a strange male hanging around in a neighbouring grove of trees. The stranger’s intentions were quite obvious: he was sizing up the group in order to join it. If he succeeded, it was more than likely that the incumbent male would be ousted from his position of privilege. With the vervet equivalent of a stroke of genius, the male hit on the ideal ploy to keep the stranger away from his group. As soon as the strange male descended from the grove of trees to try to cross the open ground that separated his grove from the one in which the group was feeding, he gave an alarm call that vervets use to signal the sighting of a leopard nearby. The stranger shot back into the safety of his trees. As the day wore on, this was repeated every time the stranger made a move in the groups direction. All was going swimmingly until the male made a crucial mistake: after successfully using the ploy several times, he gave the leopard alarm call while himself nonchalantly walking across open ground.

What Cats Catch

In a recent survey, people in the 173-household English village of Felmersham collected their cats’ prey. Over one year their seventy cats produced over 1,000 prey items. A professor in America saw these figures and worked out that on this basis the cat population of Britain must be killing 100 million birds and small mammals each year!
The mesmeric effect of big numbers seems to have stultified reason. It is not realistic just to multiply the number of catches of these rural cats by the entire cat population of Britain. Most cats are town cats with small ranges, and catch fewer items of prey than the cats in this survey. The key question should have been this: are the numbers sustainable? The answer would seem to be yes.
In winter many householders feed birds, while garden trees and buildings provide nesting sites, and in this way the bird population is kept at well above 'natural' levels. The survey found that the cat is a significant predator, but not that it is devastating Britain’s bird population.

Buffalo’s Day

The buffaloes are, as it were, the marshman’s lifeline, and they are cherished accordingly. At each dawn the buffaloes, who have been sleeping on the buffalo platform or quite frequently round the fire with their owners, leave, infinitely slowly and wearily, their wallowing progress continually punctuated with despairing groans, for the distant reed beds beyond the open water. For a long time they stand on the edge of the platform, groaning to each other of the infinite fatigue of the coming day, until at last the leader takes a ponderous pace forward and subsides into the water.
Once in the water a deep lassitude once more descends upon the party, as if they had by now forgotten their intention and they may wallow there with low notes of complaint for many minutes. The movements that at length remove them from the immediate vicinity of the house are so gradual as to pass practically unnoticed, but finally they are swimming, so low in the water that their noses seem held above it by a last effort of ebbing strength, their rolling eyes proclaiming that this is the end at last and that they are drowning. So, patient and protesting and more or less submerged, they spend the day among the reeds and the bulrushes, grazing leisurely upon such green shoots as their antediluvian heads may find at eye level.

PICASSO, Pablo 

The soles 1940 Oil on canvas Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art

Picasso tended to paint those things that surrounded him, and in the early spring of 1940, he painted several fish still lifes while he was staying in the fishing port of Royan. The ostensible subject of the painting is a fishmonger's slab with a crab, and a pair of scales containing two or three soles. In spite of their predicament these sea creatures look very much still alive. It is not very easy to read the painting because Picasso has treated the composition in terms of a flat pattern of overlapping and interlocking transparent planes. This, the thin delicately brushed paint, and the cool, undemonstrative colours give the painting the appearance of an underwater world of slow-moving calm and harmony. But this is disturbed by what seems to be an impending battle between the fish, baring their teeth, and the crab, with its open claws. Those sharp, pointed forms are echoed by the scales. Even the chain going round one of the fish takes on a more sinister aspect. There is an undercurrent of menace and barely suppressed violence that gives the picture a symbolic edge.

Vervet apen

Cheney en Seyfarth beschrijven hoe de dominante mannetjes van de groep vervet apen die ze bestudeerden, op een dag een vreemde mannetjes in een naburige boomgroep opmerkten. De bedoelingen van de vreemde mannetjes waren duidelijk: hij wilde zich bij de groep voegen. Als hij slaagde, was het waarschijnlijk dat de huidige mannetjes uit hun positie van voordeel zouden worden verjaagd. Met het vervet equivalent van een genieaals idee bedacht de mannetjes een list om de vreemde mannetjes weg te houden van zijn groep. Zodra de vreemde mannetjes vanuit de boomgroep naar beneden kwamen om te proberen de open ruimte te oversteken die de groep scheidde, gaf hij een waarschuwingssignaal dat vervets gebruiken om de nabijheid van een luipaard te signaleren. De vreemde mannetjes schoten terug naar de veiligheid van hun bomen. Naarmate de dag vorderde, werd dit herhaald telkens als de vreemde mannetjes een beweging in de richting van de groep maakten. Alles verliep prima totdat de mannetjes een cruciale fout maakten: na het succesvol gebruiken van de list een paar keer, gaf hij het leeuwenalarm terwijl hij zelf nonchalant over het open terrein liep. Wat katten vangen

In een recente enquête verzamelden mensen in het Engelse dorp Felmersham met 173 huishoudens de prooien van hun katten. In de loop van een jaar produceerden hun zeventig katten meer dan 1.000 prooien. Een professor in Amerika zag deze cijfers en berekende dat op basis hiervan de katpopulatie van Groot-Brittannië elk jaar 100 miljoen vogels en kleine zoogdieren moet doden!
De hypnotiserende werking van grote aantallen lijkt de rede te hebben verlamd. Het is niet realistisch om de aantallen van de vangsten van deze plattelandskatten te vermenigvuldigen met de gehele katpopulatie van Groot-Brittannië. De meeste katten zijn huiskatten met een klein gebied, en vangen minder prooien dan de katten in deze enquête. De belangrijkste vraag zou moeten zijn: zijn de aantallen houdbaar? Het antwoord lijkt ja te zijn. In de winter voeren veel huishoudens vogels, terwijl boomkwekerijen en gebouwen nestelplaatsen bieden en op deze manier de vogelpopulatie boven het 'natuurlijke' niveau houdt. De enquête vond dat de kat een belangrijke predator is, maar niet dat deze de vogelpopulatie in Groot-Brittannië aan het uitroeien is. Buffel's dag

De buffels zijn, als het ware, het levenslijntje van de marshman, en ze worden dienovereenkomstig gewaardeerd. Bij elke dageraad verlaten de buffels, die de nacht hebben doorgebracht op het buffelplatform of, vaak, rond het vuur met hun eigenaren, met een ongelooflijk traag en vermoeid voortkruipend tempo, hun waddengebied, waarbij hun voortgang voortdurend wordt onderbroken door wanhoopsgeluiden, totdat de leider eindelijk een zware stap voorwaarts zet en in het water neervalt.
Naar het water toe gaan de buffels, zo traag dat het bijna onopgemerkt blijft, en ze kunnen er een lange tijd liggen liggen met treurige klaagzangen, totdat ze uiteindelijk zwemmen. Ze zwemmen zo laag in het water dat hun neus er bijna bovenuit steekt door een laatste inspanning van het wegebbende kracht, hun rollende ogen verklaren dat dit het einde is en dat ze drijven. Zo patiënt en protesterend en min of meer ondergedompeld brengen ze de dag door in de rietkragen en de bulrushes, terwijl ze zich met een rustig tempo voeden met groene scheuten die op ooghoogte te vinden zijn. PICASSO, Pablo

De soles 1940 Olieverf op doek Schotse Nationale Galerie van Moderne Kunst

Picasso schilderde graag de dingen die hem omringden, en in het vroege voorjaar van 1940 schilderde hij verschillende schilderijen van visstillevens terwijl hij in de vissershaven van Royan verbleef. Het voornaamste onderwerp van het schilderij is een slagerijtafel met een krab en een paar weegschalen met twee of drie tongen. Ondanks hun benarde situatie zien deze zeedieren er nog steeds levendig uit. Het is niet erg eenvoudig om het schilderij te lezen omdat Picasso de compositie heeft behandeld in termen van een plat patroon van overlappende en in elkaar grijpende transparante vlakken. Deze, de fijne, met een kwastje aangebrachte verf en de koele, niet-demonstratieve kleuren geven het schilderij het uiterlijk van een onderwaterwereld van traag bewegende kalmte en harmonie. Maar dit wordt verstoord door wat er lijkt te gebeuren tussen de vissen, die hun tanden bared en de krab, met zijn open klauwen. Die scherpe, punctuele vormen worden geëchoerd door de weegschalen. Zelfs de ketting die om een van de vissen hangt krijgt een meer sinistere uitstraling. Er is een onderstroom van geweld en bijna onderdrukte agressie die het schilderij een symbolische lading geeft.

Vervet monkeys

Cheney and Seyfarth describe how one day the dominant male in the group of vervet monkeys they were studying noticed a strange male hanging around in a neighbouring grove of trees. The stranger’s intentions were quite obvious: he was sizing up the group in order to join it. If he succeeded, it was more than likely that the incumbent male would be ousted from his position of privilege. With the vervet equivalent of a stroke of genius, the male hit on the ideal ploy to keep the stranger away from his group. As soon as the strange male descended from the grove of trees to try to cross the open ground that separated his grove from the one in which the group was feeding, he gave an alarm call that vervets use to signal the sighting of a leopard nearby. The stranger shot back into the safety of his trees. As the day wore on, this was repeated every time the stranger made a move in the groups direction. All was going swimmingly until the male made a crucial mistake: after successfully using the ploy several times, he gave the leopard alarm call while himself nonchalantly walking across open ground.

What Cats Catch

In a recent survey, people in the 173-household English village of Felmersham collected their cats’ prey. Over one year their seventy cats produced over 1,000 prey items. A professor in America saw these figures and worked out that on this basis the cat population of Britain must be killing 100 million birds and small mammals each year!
The mesmeric effect of big numbers seems to have stultified reason. It is not realistic just to multiply the number of catches of these rural cats by the entire cat population of Britain. Most cats are town cats with small ranges, and catch fewer items of prey than the cats in this survey. The key question should have been this: are the numbers sustainable? The answer would seem to be yes.
In winter many householders feed birds, while garden trees and buildings provide nesting sites, and in this way the bird population is kept at well above 'natural' levels. The survey found that the cat is a significant predator, but not that it is devastating Britain’s bird population.

Buffalo’s Day

The buffaloes are, as it were, the marshman’s lifeline, and they are cherished accordingly. At each dawn the buffaloes, who have been sleeping on the buffalo platform or quite frequently round the fire with their owners, leave, infinitely slowly and wearily, their wallowing progress continually punctuated with despairing groans, for the distant reed beds beyond the open water. For a long time they stand on the edge of the platform, groaning to each other of the infinite fatigue of the coming day, until at last the leader takes a ponderous pace forward and subsides into the water.
Once in the water a deep lassitude once more descends upon the party, as if they had by now forgotten their intention and they may wallow there with low notes of complaint for many minutes. The movements that at length remove them from the immediate vicinity of the house are so gradual as to pass practically unnoticed, but finally they are swimming, so low in the water that their noses seem held above it by a last effort of ebbing strength, their rolling eyes proclaiming that this is the end at last and that they are drowning. So, patient and protesting and more or less submerged, they spend the day among the reeds and the bulrushes, grazing leisurely upon such green shoots as their antediluvian heads may find at eye level.

PICASSO, Pablo 

The soles 1940 Oil on canvas Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art

Picasso tended to paint those things that surrounded him, and in the early spring of 1940, he painted several fish still lifes while he was staying in the fishing port of Royan. The ostensible subject of the painting is a fishmonger's slab with a crab, and a pair of scales containing two or three soles. In spite of their predicament these sea creatures look very much still alive. It is not very easy to read the painting because Picasso has treated the composition in terms of a flat pattern of overlapping and interlocking transparent planes. This, the thin delicately brushed paint, and the cool, undemonstrative colours give the painting the appearance of an underwater world of slow-moving calm and harmony. But this is disturbed by what seems to be an impending battle between the fish, baring their teeth, and the crab, with its open claws. Those sharp, pointed forms are echoed by the scales. Even the chain going round one of the fish takes on a more sinister aspect. There is an undercurrent of menace and barely suppressed violence that gives the picture a symbolic edge.

Singes vervet

Cheney et Seyfarth décrivent comment un jour le mâle dominant du groupe de singes vervet qu'ils étudiaient a remarqué un mâle étranger qui se promenait dans un bosquet d'arbres voisin. Les intentions de l'étranger étaient évidentes : il évaluait le groupe afin de pouvoir y rejoindre. S'il y parvenait, il était fort probable que le mâle en place serait chassé de son poste de privilège. Avec l'équivalent des singes vervet d'un coup de génie, le mâle a trouvé le subterfuge idéal pour empêcher l'étranger d'approcher de son groupe. Dès que l'étranger descendait du bosquet d'arbres pour essayer de traverser l'espace ouvert qui séparait son bosquet de celui où le groupe se nourrissait, il donnait un appel d'alarme que les singes vervet utilisent pour signaler la présence d'un léopard à proximité. L'étranger repartait aussitôt dans le sécurité de son bosquet. Au fil de la journée, cela se reproduisait à chaque fois que l'étranger se dirigeait vers le groupe. Tout se passait bien jusqu'à ce que le mâle fasse une erreur cruciale : après avoir réussi à utiliser le subterfuge plusieurs fois, il donnait l'appel d'alarme du léopard tout en marchant lui-même sans problème sur l'espace ouvert.

Qu'attrapent les chats

Dans une enquête récente, les habitants de la petite ville anglaise de Felmersham ont collecté la proie de leurs chats. Au cours d'une année, leurs soixante-dix chats ont produit plus de 1 000 proies. Un professeur en Amérique a vu ces chiffres et a calculé que, sur cette base, la population de chats de Grande-Bretagne doit tuer 100 millions d'oiseaux et de petits mammifères par an! L'effet hypnotique des grands nombres semble avoir paralysé la raison. Il n'est pas réaliste de multiplier le nombre de prises de ces chats de campagne par l'ensemble de la population de chats de Grande-Bretagne. La plupart des chats sont des chats de ville avec de petits territoires, et ils capturent moins d'objets de proie que les chats de cette étude. La question clé aurait dû être la suivante : ces chiffres sont-ils durables? La réponse semble être oui. En hiver, de nombreux propriétaires de chats nourrissent les oiseaux, tandis que les arbres des jardins et les bâtiments fournissent des sites de nidification, et de cette manière, la population d'oiseaux est maintenue bien au-dessus du niveau « naturel ». L'enquête a montré que le chat est un prédateur important, mais pas qu'il est en train de détruire la population d'oiseaux de Grande-Bretagne.

Le jour du buffle

Les buffles sont, pour ainsi dire, la source de vie du maraîcher, et ils sont chéris en conséquence. À chaque matinée, les buffles, qui ont dormi sur la plate-forme des buffles ou, très souvent, autour du feu avec leurs propriétaires, quittent, infiniment lentement et avec une lassitude extrême, leur marche dans l'eau, leur progression continuellement ponctuée de grognements désespérés, jusqu'aux roseaux lointains au-delà de l'eau ouverte. Pendant longtemps, ils se tiennent sur le bord de la plate-forme, grognant les uns aux autres du lassitude infinie de la journée à venir, jusqu'à ce que finalement le chef fasse un pas lent et s'abîme dans l'eau. Une fois dans l'eau, une lassitude profonde redescend à nouveau sur le groupe, comme s'ils avaient déjà oublié leur intention et qu'ils peuvent nager là-bas avec des notes de plainte prolongées pendant de nombreuses minutes. Les mouvements qui finalement les éloignent de la maison sont si graduels qu'ils passent pratiquement inaperçus, mais finalement, ils nagent, si bas dans l'eau que leurs nez semblent maintenus au-dessus d'elle par un dernier effort d'épuisement, leurs yeux roulants proclamant que c'est la fin enfin et qu'ils sont en train de se noyer. Ainsi, patients et en colère et plus ou moins submergés, ils passent la journée parmi les roseaux et les bulrushes, mangeant tranquillement des pousses vertes à la verticale de leurs yeux. PICASSO, Pablo

Les soles 1940 Huile sur toile Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art

Picasso avait tendance à peindre ce qui l'entourait, et au début du printemps 1940, il a peint plusieurs tableaux de poissons alors qu'il séjournait dans le port de pêche de Royan. Le sujet apparent de la peinture est une table de boucher avec un crabe, et une paire de balances contenant deux ou trois soles. En dépit de leur situation, ces créatures marines semblent toujours vivantes. Il n'est pas très facile de lire la peinture car Picasso a traité la composition en termes d'un motif plat de plans transparents superposés. Ceci, la peinture délicatement brossée et les couleurs froides et indifférentes donnent à la peinture l'apparence d'un monde sous-marin de mouvement lent et harmonieux. Mais cela est perturbé par ce qui semble être une bataille imminente entre les poissons, barrant leurs dents, et le crabe, avec ses pattes ouvertes. Ces formes pointues sont reprises par les balances. Même la chaîne qui tourne autour d'un des poissons prend une apparence plus sinistre. Il y a un sous-sol d'agressivité et de violence à peine supprimée qui donne à la peinture une symbolique d'arête.

Slowly, Gabriel went up the stairs to the Delgados' flat. The building
was dangerous, but he didn't think about that. He could hear the cries of
the child. He felt terrible. Then he felt something on the floor under his
foot. He looked down. It was his red rose. It was there, in the same place,
by the front door. A rose from another world, another life.
The door of the flat was open. Gabriel called, 'Mrs Delgado! Silvia! Are you there?'
There was no answer, but suddenly, two men ran out of the sitting-room.
The first man went down the stairs before Gabriel could stop him.
Then the other man ran past. Gabriel put out his foot and the man fell
over it. A box fell to the ground. The man didn't stop. He jumped up
and ran away.
Gabriel opened the box. There was jewellery inside it.
'Mrs. Delgado's jewellery!' he thought. 'So the thieves are busy now!'
He took the jewellery box into the flat. He looked round. The pictures
were on the walls. Silvia's camera was on the table.
'Good,' he thought. 'The thieves didn't have much time. They only took the jewellery, and I've got it now.'
Then, near one of the armchairs, he saw Silvia's dirty evening shoes. He thought for a minute. For the first time for hours, he smiled. 'She wore those shoes last night,' he thought. 'So she came back here after the earthquake. She isn't dead! She came home, and took her mother to a safe place. Oh Silvia, Silvia, you're all right!'

Art on TV

Why is it that television so consistently fails when it comes to programmes about the visual arts? Painting and sculpture should be natural subjects for the camera, which has the ability to show a whole work of art, then move in close to examine the details. Yet I can think of few series on television that have managed to convey both the pleasure and complexity of looking at them.
A good example of what goes wrong can be seen in Robert Hughes’s eight part survey of American art, American Visions. Hughes is a critic you can trust, he has a personality that commands attention and he has been given nearly eight hours in which to introduce British audiences to a school of art that British galleries have totally ignored. I had expected the series to focus on great works of art. What I got instead was one about the way American history and culture are reflected in its art and architecture.

Dealing in Metals

For 20 years I worked as an international metals dealer and gained something of a reputation as a speculator. Metals are regulated far less than other markets. With a bit of luck, a willingness to take a risk and a good understanding of how the market works, it’s possible to make a lot of money. Risk-taking is part and parcel of the industry. The buccaneering culture fits nicely with a free-market global economy. But now the free-trade economists who claimed the market itself would maintain the price of scarce metals have found the opposite is happening. More minerals are being extracted and the cost of raw materials is decreasing. Taking inflation into account, the prices of most metals are about half of what they were 20 years ago. Recently, I was asked to look into allegations made against one of the multinational conglomerates that benefit from these cheap raw materials.

Extract from a Holiday Brochure

Abaco and its off-shore cays are part of the 700 islands of the Bahamas that stretch from Florida past the Tropic of Cancer, to Cuba. Each one has its own personality, each one has something to offer.
The key to getting anywhere in the islands and cays of Abaco is a boat. If you don’t get one thrown in with the room don’t worry. Be happy. There are ferries galore. And water-taxis. Or, there are plenty of boats to rent if you prefer to go under your own steam.
But sailing is the most popular mode of transport here. Abaco is nicknamed ‘The Sailing Capital of the World' for good reason.
Those calm, naturally protected waters are also a paradise for fishing, diving, snorkelling and swimming. The cays and their beaches stretch for 200 miles like a string of pearls. It’s not only at sea that gems can be found. At night it's the lights of the restaurants and cafes of Hope Town and Green Turtle Cay that sparkle.
results.tgt_text:
Kunst op tv

Waarom lukt het televisie zo vaak niet als het gaat om programma's over beeldende kunst? Schilderkunst en beeldhouwkunst zouden natuurlijk een logische onderwerpen zijn voor de camera, die het mogelijk maakt een heel kunstwerk te tonen en vervolgens in te zoomen op de details. Toch kan ik me maar weinig series op televisie herinneren die erin zijn geslaagd zowel het plezier als de complexiteit van het kijken naar kunst over te brengen.
Een goed voorbeeld van wat er mis kan gaan is te zien in de achtdelige serie van Robert Hughes over Amerikaanse kunst, American Visions. Hughes is een criticus waar je op kunt vertrouwen, hij heeft een persoonlijkheid die aandacht opeist en hij kreeg bijna acht uur om het Britse publiek kennis te laten maken met een school van kunst die door Britse galerieën volledig is genegeerd. Ik had verwacht dat de serie zich zou richten op grote kunstwerken. Wat ik kreeg was een serie over de manier waarop de Amerikaanse geschiedenis en cultuur in de kunst en architectuur van Amerika zijn weerspiegeld.

Handel in metalen

Ik heb 20 jaar lang gewerkt als internationaal handelaar in metalen en heb een beetje een reputatie opgebouwd als speculant. Metalen worden veel minder gereguleerd dan andere markten. Met een beetje geluk, de bereidheid om een risico te nemen en een goed begrip van hoe de markt werkt, is het mogelijk veel geld te verdienen. Risicovol gedrag is een integraal onderdeel van de industrie. De buccaneer-cultuur past goed bij een vrije wereldwijde markteconomie. Maar nu hebben de vrije-handels-economen die beweerden dat de markt zelf de prijs van schaarse metalen zou handhaven, het tegendeel ontdekt. Er worden meer mineralen gewonnen en de kosten van grondstoffen nemen af. Rekening houdend met inflatie zijn de prijzen van de meeste metalen ongeveer de helft van wat ze 20 jaar geleden waren. Onlangs werd ik gevraagd om onderzoek te doen naar beschuldigingen tegen een van de multinationale conglomeraten die profiteren van deze goedkope grondstoffen.

Uit een vakantiebrochure

Abaco en de off-shore cays behoren tot de 700 eilanden van de Bahama's die zich uitstrekken van Florida voorbij de evenaar tot Cuba. Elk eiland heeft zijn eigen persoonlijkheid, elk eiland heeft iets te bieden.
Het sleutelwoord voor het bereiken van de eilanden en cays van Abaco is een boot. Als je er niet een krijgt die met de kamer wordt meegeleverd, maak je je geen zorgen. Wees blij. Er zijn veerboten te over. En water-taxis. Of je kunt genoeg boten huren als je liever onder eigen stuur wilt varen.
Maar varen is de populairste manier van vervoer hier. Abaco staat ook wel bekend als 'De Zeilhoofdstad van de Wereld' en dat is niet voor niets.
De kalme, natuurlijke beschermde wateren zijn ook een paradijs voor vissen, duiken, snorkelen en zwemmen. De cays en hun stranden strekken zich uit over 200 mijl als een rij parels. Het is niet alleen op zee dat edelstenen te vinden zijn.'s Nachts is het de lichten van de restaurants en cafés van Hope Town en Green Turtle Cay die schitteren.

L'art à la télévision

Pourquoi la télévision est-elle si constamment défaillante lorsqu'il s'agit de programmes sur les arts visuels? La peinture et la sculpture devraient être des sujets naturels pour la caméra, qui a la capacité de montrer une œuvre d'art entière, puis de s'approcher pour examiner les détails. Pourtant, je peux penser à peu de séries à la télévision qui ont réussi à transmettre à la fois le plaisir et la complexité de les regarder. Un bon exemple de ce qui ne fonctionne pas peut être vu dans American Visions, l'enquête en huit parties de Robert Hughes sur l'art américain. Hughes est un critique auquel on peut faire confiance, il a une personnalité qui attire l'attention et il a été autorisé à présenter aux Britanniques une école d'art que les galeries britanniques ont totalement ignorée. J'avais espéré que la série se concentrerait sur les grandes œuvres d'art. Au lieu de cela, j'ai obtenu une série sur la façon dont l'histoire et la culture américaines se reflètent dans son art et son architecture.

Avec un peu de chance, une volonté de prendre des risques et une bonne compréhension de la façon dont fonctionne le marché, il est possible de gagner beaucoup d'argent. Le risque est une partie intégrante de l'industrie. La culture de la piraterie s'accorde bien avec une économie mondiale de libre-échange. Mais maintenant, les économistes partisans du libre-échange qui prétendaient que le marché lui-même maintenait le prix des métaux rares ont découvert que l'inverse se produit. Plus de minéraux sont extraits et le coût des matières premières diminue. En tenant compte de l'inflation, les prix de la plupart des métaux sont d'environ la moitié de ce qu'ils étaient il y a 20 ans. Récemment, on m'a demandé d'enquêter sur des allégations portées contre l'un des conglomérats multinationales qui bénéficient de ces matières premières bon marché.

Abaco et ses cayes au large font partie des 700 îles des Bahamas qui s'étendent de la Floride au-delà du tropique du Cancer jusqu'à Cuba. Chaque île a sa propre personnalité, chacune a quelque chose à offrir.
La clé pour se rendre n'importe où dans les îles et les cayes d'Abaco est un bateau. Si vous ne vous en procurer un avec la chambre, ne vous inquiétez pas. Soyez heureux. La nuit, ce sont les lumières des restaurants et des cafés de Hope Town et de Green Turtle Cay qui brillent.

The History of Farming 

Before people started farming, they went to the forest to look for plants or fruit they could eat. This meant that people were moving all the time to find food. But about 12,000 years ago, in the Middle East, people began to grow food. These people were the first farmers. Farming made it possible for people to stay in one place and slowly their villages got bigger. 
Some people in the villages became free to do other work, like making clothes, because the farmers could grow food for everyone. Unfortunately, farming was difficult when the weather was bad and then some people did not get enough food to eat. 
Today, farmers can grow more food and it travels thousands of kilometres from where it is grown to our homes.
results.tgt_text:
De geschiedenis van de landbouw

Voordat mensen begonnen met landbouw gingen ze naar het bos om planten of fruit te zoeken om te eten. Hierdoor moesten mensen voortdurend verhuizen om voedsel te vinden. Maar ongeveer 12.000 jaar geleden begonnen mensen in het Midden-Oosten met het verbouwen van voedsel. Deze mensen waren de eerste boeren. Door de landbouw konden mensen op één plek blijven wonen en werden hun dorpen steeds groter. Sommige mensen in de dorpen konden zich bezig houden met andere werkzaamheden, zoals het maken van kleren, omdat de boeren genoeg voedsel konden verbouwen voor iedereen. Helaas was landbouw moeilijk wanneer het weer slecht was en kregen sommige mensen dan niet genoeg voedsel om te eten. Tegenwoordig kunnen boeren meer voedsel verbouwen en reist het voedsel duizenden kilometers van waar het wordt verbouwd naar onze huizen.

Watering the Desert
 It can rain at any time between November and March in Marrakesh, Morocco. It doesn’t happen frequently and when it does, the city’s water pipes can’t manage the sudden floods, which turn the streets into rivers. But, as many winters have remained dry in recent times, when the rain does come, it is welcomed by the local people. 
Marrakesh’s parks and gardens exist, not because of the rain, but thanks to a network of underground channels, dug in the 11th century, which bring in water from the mountains all year round. Basically dry places, which receive their water in this way, are known as oases. 
Further south from Marrakesh, the traveller arrives at Skoura. Here every available piece of land is made into small squares by the water channels and used to grow food. The Atlas mountains, snow-covered in winter, provide a delightful background.

In Marrakesh, Marokko kan het tussen november en maart op elk moment regenen. Het gebeurt niet vaak en als het wel regent, kunnen de waterleidingen van de stad de plotselinge overstromingen niet aan. De straten worden dan rivieren. Maar omdat de winters de laatste tijd droog zijn gebleven, wordt de regen door de lokale bevolking verwelkomd.
De parken en tuinen van Marrakesh bestaan niet door de regen, maar dankzij een netwerk van ondergrondse kanalen die in de 11e eeuw zijn gegraven en het hele jaar door water uit de bergen brengen. Droge plekken die op deze manier water krijgen, heten oases.
Verder naar het zuiden van Marrakesh komt de reiziger in Skoura. Hier wordt elk stukje beschikbare grond bewaterd door waterkanalen en gebruikt om voedsel te verbouwen. De besneeuwde Atlasgebergte vormt een prachtige achtergrond.

I stopped the car in a cloud of dust, and we walked up the steps and into the saloon. 
Well if I'd wanted to do a bit of time-travelling, I couldn't have done much better; walking through that door was like walking back eighty years in time. Inside, the old Western saloon was still intact, with its big long wooden bar, and enormous mirrors on the walls. Apart from the electric light, the juke box, and the tables set for dinner, it was almost perfect. 
And there in the corner sat the prospector, with his wife. If he'd been wearing a red gown, I'd have taken him for Father Christmas, but he wasn't. This old-timer wasn't in Atlantic City to bring presents, but to find gold. 

He said his name was Brad, and he'd been looking for gold in Atlantic City for some time now. Yes, he'd found some too; not enough to make him a millionaire, but enough to make him happy. 
When the Gold Rush ended in Atlantic City, he told me, it was not actually because there was no more gold, but because gold was too hard to find, or not valuable enough. 
Today, gold is a lot more valuable than it was a hundred years ago, and modern techniques allow people to find gold more easily. And that was why Brad and his wife were in Atlantic City, digging for gold. 
They were not the only ones, said Brad; quite a few of the "concessions" are now being worked, and some old mines are being opened up again. In some places, mining for gold has become commercially profitable again; but in most cases, the miners, like Brad, are just amateurs.

Yes, he had found it too; not enough to make him a millionaire, but enough to make him happy. When the gold rush ended in Atlantic City, he said, it wasn't because there was no more gold, but because the gold was too hard to find, or not valuable enough. Today, gold is worth a lot more than it was a hundred years ago, and modern techniques make it easier for people to find gold. And that's why Brad and his wife were in Atlantic City, digging for gold. They weren't the only ones, Brad said; a number of "claims" are now being worked, and some old mines are being reopened. GETTING FIT 

Exercise is essential for mind, body and spirit. It's one of the best ways to maintain a perfect balance when all around you everything seems more and more unbalanced and the world becomes ever more fast and furious. 
Don't groan because this is yet another article about fitness. The reason why there are so many is that it is seriously good for you. There are plenty of reasons why you should exercise and very few - for most of us why you shouldn't. Exercise improves muscle tone and provides quick changes in body shape. It improves muscle power and promotes good posture - the way in which you hold your body when sitting or standing. It helps prevent those muscle imbalances which can lead to injuries. It provides quick improvement in specific problem areas such as thighs, stomach and upper arms. It improves the condition of the heart and lungs and blood circulation. 
Probably all these reasons have been thrown at you time and time again, so maybe you are bored by them and have switched off. All right then, this should make you sit up and take notice. Did you know that exercise helps to ease depression and tiredness, and that it helps to regulate sleep patterns? Also that exercise is instrumental in controlling stress? Not only this, but exercise can help to relieve certain medical conditions. 
By now you should be influenced a little by these arguments. If not, common sense alone should tell you that exercise is good for you. 
There are plenty of types of exercise you can do aerobics, calisthenics, jogging, working out with free weights, working on weight machines. There is one point you should note - training too hard and with too much weight may cause injury, so start slowly and carefully. If you're not sure, you should consult your doctor on what's good for you personally. 
No amount of exercise will improve your body shape if you don't have good posture. This practically determines how you look and feel. Not only is a stiff or sagging body unattractive, it also lacks energy and is more likely to suffer from minor health complaints. 
If your body tends to slouch, imagine that the top of your head is connected to a helium balloon, which is trying to pull you up into the sky. This will help you to lift the chest for fuller and easier breathing. At the same time, it lengthens the abdomen, making the body look much slimmer. If the chest is well balanced when you are standing, you can see your ankles. 
Stretching the muscles improves flexibility and ease of movement, and helps you to maintain correct posture and to prevent muscle tears and injuries caused by overuse. If done four or five times a week, it will guarantee a more flexible,fitter body. So stretching should play an important part in your exercise routine, which should be performed both slowly and precisely. 
The best exercise, therefore, involves a good warm-up, stretching exercises, an energetic workout and definitely a cool down period.

Elliott hid in some plants by the road with Harvey and watched the scientists' vans. They drove up and down the streets, and then out into
the forest. Their lights shone in the night sky. "Harvey," Elliott said quietly, "we have something wonderful with us. Do you know that? I love him, Harvey." He looked up at the sky. Which star did his new friend come from? His little eyes shone and they looked carefully at Elliott. Lance knew something, and Elliott was afraid. Elliott and Michael walked to school. 
"We have to tell, Elliott," Michael said. "No," Elliott answered. "He wants to stay with us. Michael, listen, there are some strange people around here now. I don't know them. Look at that car. There's a man inside it and he's reading a newspaper. Why is he there? What's he waiting for? I think they're looking for E.T."
Elliott was very unhappy. "Michael," he said, "we can't tell, or he won't get back home. I know it-I can feel it inside me." Greg, Tyler, and Steve were at the bus stop. "Elliott, what happened to your 'little man' in the yard? Did he come
back?" Steve asked him. "Yes, he came back," Elliott said too quickly.

There was an old gas fire in the room. The fire wasn't lit, and there was gas in the room. His candle lit the gas. There was a very loud noise ... and then a fire started. He died in the fire.'

And certainly Catherine's education could not be described as appropriate for a heroine. In fact, she had an obvious dislike for the classroom and never could learn or understand anything before she was taught; occasionally she even seemed rather stupid. 
Her mother wanted her to learn music and Catherine was sure that she would like to play the piano, so at eight years old she began lessons. But she soon gave up, and the day on which the music teacher was dismissed was one of the happiest days of her young life. Her drawing ability was also disappointing; although she enjoyed drawing animals, all her pictures, from chickens to horses, looked very similar. 
What a strange, incomprehensible character! Incomprehensible because, in spite of such clear signs of a difficult nature, Catherine was seldom unpleasant; she rarely quarrelled and was very kind to her six younger brothers and sisters and quite friendly with the three older ones. But it still must be admitted that she was untidy, noisy and wild and loved nothing better than rolling down her favourite hill at the back of the house. 
At fifteen, Catherine's appearance began to improve; her skin was brighter, her hair was shinier and nicely styled, her eyes shone and her figure was pleasing. Her love of dirt was replaced by an interest in the latest fashions and in the possibility of going to a ball. She was quite thrilled one day to hear her father remark on her personal improvement: 'Catherine is almost pretty today.' To be almost pretty is a great prize to a girl who has been plain for fifteen years.

It was late autumn. The weather was wet and the wind had blown all the leaves from the trees. I was riding my horse across the wet, empty land. I was traveling alone. I was going toward a dark and strange house - the House of Usher.
Why had I come to this lonely place? I knew Roderick Usher - the owner of the house. We were old friends, but we had not met for many years. A few weeks ago, I had received a letter from Roderick.

I am ill - very ill. Please come and visit me. I am going mad! I want your help. We have been friends since we were boys. Please come!
Roderick Usher

I had been riding all day and it was now late. The pale sun was low in the sky when I arrived at the House of Usher.
A large lake of black water surrounded the house. I stopped by the lake and looked at the house. Roderick Usher's house was a large black building. Its many windows were like empty eyes. Suddenly, I felt cold...and a little afraid.
In front of me, a narrow road went across a bridge toward the house. I walked my horse along the narrow road until I reached the walls of the house.
I knocked on the front door and a servant opened it. He took my horse to a stable. Then he led me inside the house.
We climbed many stairs to his master's room. Lamps burned along the walls, but they gave little light. The long corridors and stairways were full of dark shadows.
The servant opened a big, wooden door and I looked inside a large room.

THE HISTORY OF THE LONDON POLICE

Today there are policemen everywhere, but in 1700 London had no policemen at all. A few old men used to protect the city streets at night and they were not paid very much.
About 300 years ago, London was starting to get bigger. The city was very dirty and many people were poor. There were so many thieves who stole money in the streets that people stayed in their homes as much as possible.
In 1750, Henry Fielding started to pay a group of people to stop thieves. They were like policemen and were called 'Bow Street Runners' because they worked near Bow Street.
Fifty years later, there were 120 Bow Street Runners, but London had become very big and needed more policemen. So, in 1829, the first Metropolitan (or London) Police Force was started with 3000 officers. Most of the men worked on foot, but a few rode horses. Until 1920 all the police in London were men.
Today, London police are quite well paid and for the few police officers who still ride horses, the pay is even better than for the others.

Once a select forum of the great and good, the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference now has millions of avid online fans. How did an elite ideas-sharing gathering go mainstream?
Falling animals, misbehaving toddlers and footage of Justin Bieber may populate the bulk of any YouTube most-viewed list.
But amid the viral clips and pop music promos is a series of videos that seems to go against all received wisdom about what online audiences like to consume.
Their tone is sunnily optimistic, go-getting, Californian, with titles like Information Is Food, Crowdsource Your Health and Inventing Is the Easy Part.
They feature luminaries such as Stephen Hawking, JK Rowling and Bono delivering 18-minute lectures about big ideas - technology, culture, the environment, science, social trends.
Yet although there is nary a Lolcat in sight, the YouTube channel of the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference has attracted nearly 112 million views.
The talks have a habit of catching on. TED attendees were given a preview of Al Gore's lecture on climate change lecture, later popularised in An Inconvenient Truth . Biologist Richard Dawkins' 2002 lecture on "militant atheism" laid the groundwork for the arguments set out in hishugely controversial book The God Delusion 
Others have entered the realms of the downright strange, such as whenMicrosoft founder Bill Gates unleashed live mosquitoes into the auditorium during a talk on malaria because "there's no reason why only poor people should have the experience" (the insects were not infected).
It's an impressive level of public interest in an event sneered at by detractors as an expensive talking-shop-cum-networking-event for latte-wielding, iPad clutching, West Coast blue-sky thinkers.

Falling animals, misbehaving toddlers and footage of Justin Bieber may populate the bulk of any YouTube most-viewed list.
But amid the viral clips and pop music promos is a series of videos that seems to go against all received wisdom about what online audiences like to consume.
Their tone is sunnily optimistic, go-getting, Californian, with titles like Information Is Food, Crowdsource Your Health and Inventing Is the Easy Part.
They feature luminaries such as Stephen Hawking, JK Rowling and Bono delivering 18-minute lectures about big ideas - technology, culture, the environment, science, social trends.
Yet although there is nary a Lolcat in sight, the YouTube channel of the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference has attracted nearly 112 million views.
The talks have a habit of catching on. TED attendees were given a preview of Al Gore's lecture on climate change lecture, later popularised in An Inconvenient Truth . Biologist Richard Dawkins' 2002 lecture on "militant atheism" laid the groundwork for the arguments set out in hishugely controversial book The God Delusion 
Others have entered the realms of the downright strange, such as whenMicrosoft founder Bill Gates unleashed live mosquitoes into the auditorium during a talk on malaria because "there's no reason why only poor people should have the experience" (the insects were not infected).
It's an impressive level of public interest in an event sneered at by detractors as an expensive talking-shop-cum-networking-event for latte-wielding, iPad clutching, West Coast blue-sky thinkers.
results.tgt_text: Une fois un forum sélect de grands hommes, la conférence Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) a désormais des millions de fans avides en ligne. Comment une rencontre d'idées élitiste est-elle devenue populaire? Les animaux qui tombent, les tout-petits indisciplinés et les images de Justin Bieber peuvent remplir la majeure partie de n'importe quelle liste des vidéos les plus vues sur YouTube. Mais parmi les clips viraux et les publicités de musique pop se trouve une série de vidéos qui semble aller à l'encontre de toutes les idées reçues sur ce que les audiences en ligne aiment consommer. Leur ton est ensoleillé, optimiste, dynamique et californien, avec des titres comme Information Is Food, Crowdsource Your Health et Inventing Is the Easy Part. Elles présentent des personnalités telles que Stephen Hawking, JK Rowling et Bono qui livrent des conférences de 18 minutes sur de grandes idées - la technologie, la culture, l'environnement, la science, les tendances sociales. Cependant, il n'y a pas de Lolcat en vue. La chaîne YouTube de la conférence Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) a attiré près de 112 millions de vues. Les conférences ont tendance à se propager. Les participants à TED ont eu un avant-goût de la conférence d'Al Gore sur le changement climatique, popularisée plus tard dans An Inconvenient Truth. Le biologiste Richard Dawkins a donné une conférence en 2002 sur « l'athéisme militant » qui a jeté les bases des arguments exposés dans son livre très controversé The God Delusion. D'autres ont franchi les frontières de l'étrange, comme lorsque le fondateur de Microsoft Bill Gates a libéré des moustiques vivants dans l'auditorium lors d'une conférence sur le paludisme car « il n'y a aucune raison pour que ce soit seulement les pauvres qui aient cette expérience » (les insectes n'étaient pas infectés). C'est un niveau impressionnant d'intérêt public pour un événement méprisé par les détracteurs comme un salon de discussion et d'événement de réseautage coûteux pour les latte-wielding, iPad clutching, blue-sky thinkers de la Côte Ouest.

Among the falling animals, the unruly toddlers and the Justin Bieber images that make up much of any YouTube most-watched list, there is a series of videos that seem to go against all the received ideas about what online audiences like to consume. Their tone is sunny, optimistic, dynamic and Californian, with titles like Information Is Food, Crowdsource Your Health and Inventing Is the Easy Part. They feature personalities such as Stephen Hawking, JK Rowling and Bono delivering 18-minute talks on big ideas - technology, culture, the environment, science, social trends. But there is no Lolcat in sight. The Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) YouTube channel has attracted nearly 112 million views. TED talks tend to go viral. TED attendees got a taste of Al Gore's climate change conference, popularised later in An Inconvenient Truth. When the Mayor heard about Jack's fall from the sky, he sadly told everybody in  his town. They all looked down at the ground. They didn't scream or shout. They stood and remembered their great friend. "We will never see our dear friend Jack Skellington again," the Mayor said. 
"This is a very sad day for us all." Everybody felt very bad, but nobody was sadder than the Mayor. Sally could hear the Mayor from inside Oogie Boogie's house. He spoke loudly and she tried hard to listen to his words. They sounded very important and very sad. When Sally understood, she cried quietly. Oogie Boogie laughed at her. "Now I'm the scariest person in Halloweentown!" he shouted happily. 
"No more Jack Skellington! Yes!" Sally was in Oogie Boogie's house because she tried to help Santa Claus. Oogie Boogie caught her. He put her on another chair, next to Santa, so she couldn't get away. Oogie Boogie laughed at her, but Sally wasn't afraid.  "You can laugh now," she said to him angrily. "But you'll be sorry!" Oogie laughed again. 
"Very funny, Sally!" he said. But Jack's life didn't end when his sleigh hit the ground. He ran as fast as he could through the woods, with Zero behind him. Then he heard Oogie Boogie's laugh under the ground and stopped suddenly. He looked down the hole to Oogie Boogie's house and he could see Santa and Sally in the chairs and the hungry Oogie Boogie by the fire.

Almost everyone knows the story of “Peter Pan” which is why this is an easy read. Being familiar with a story already helps the reader to understand the text better. This book is aimed at children, but it continues to be enjoyed by adults around the world too.
Plot Summary
Every night Peter visits the Darling family house and listens to Mrs. Darling tell bedtime stories. He sits on the window listening. One evening, they see Peter trying to escape. As he tries to run away, he loses his shadow. He goes back to get his shadow. He wakes up the daughter of the house, Wendy Darling. Wendy helps him attach his shadow to his body again. Wendy tells him she knows a lot of bedtime stories too.
Peter invites Wendy to return to Neverland with him. He wants her to be the mother of the Lost Boys. Wendy agrees to the mission and asks for her brothers Michael and John to join them.
They have a magical flight as they travel to Neverland and have many adventures along the way. Wendy is nearly killed and the boys build her a house in the trees to recover. After Wendy is okay, she takes the role of the mother.
After all their adventures and fun, Wendy decides that her place is at home with their mother. Wendy helps all the Lost Boys return to London. But Peter doesn’t want her to go. Instead he tries to trick her. He tells her that their mother doesn’t want them anymore. However, he understands how sad their mother must be. In the end, he decides to let them go home.
results.tgt_text: Nagenoeg iedereen kent het verhaal van ‘Peter Pan’, waardoor dit een gemakkelijke leeservaring is. Het feit dat je bekend bent met een verhaal helpt de lezer om de tekst beter te begrijpen. Dit boek is bedoeld voor kinderen, maar wordt nog steeds door volwassenen over de hele wereld met plezier gelezen.
results.back_text: Nearly everyone knows the story of ‘Peter Pan’, which makes this an easy read. The fact that you are familiar with a story helps the reader to understand the text better. This book is intended for children, but is still enjoyed by adults all over the world.

The journey from our town to the capital was a journey of about five hours. When I arrived at Mr Jaggers's office the clerk told me that he was in court, and that he had left word I should wait in
his room. He led me to a dark room. After I had waited for a long time Mr Jaggers arrived.
Many people, men and women, who had been waiting for him outside the office, made a rush at him. He addressed himself to two of the men.
'Now, I have nothing to say to you,' said Mr Jaggers, pointing his finger at them. 'I want to know no more than I know. As to the result, it could go either way. I told you that from the start. Have you paid Wemmick?'
'Yes, sir,' said both the men together.
'Very well; then you may go. Now, I won't have it!' said Mr Jaggers, waving his hand at them to put them behind him. 'If you say a word to me, I'll throw up the case.'
'We thought, Mr Jaggers -' one of the men began, pulling off his hat.
'That's what I told you not to do,' said Mr Jaggers. 'You thought! I think for you; that's enough for you. If I want you, I know where to find you; I don't want you to find me. Now I won't have it. I won't hear a word.' 
The two men looked at one another as Mr Jaggers waved them behind him, and fell back and were heard no more.

Toen ik bij het kantoor van de heer Jaggers aankwam, vertelde de klerk dat hij in de rechtbank was en dat hij had gezegd dat ik moest wachten in zijn kamer. Hij bracht me naar een donkere kamer. Nadat ik lang had gewacht, kwam de heer Jaggers aan. Veel mensen, mannen en vrouwen, die buiten het kantoor op hem hadden gewacht, stormden naar hem toe. Hij sprak zich tot twee van de mannen uit. 'Nu heb ik niets meer te zeggen tegen u,' zei de heer Jaggers, terwijl hij zijn vinger op hen richtte. 'Ik weet er niets meer van. Wat het resultaat betreft, het kan alle kanten op. Ik heb u dat vanaf het begin gezegd. Hebt u Wemmick betaald?' 'Ja, meneer,' zeiden beide mannen samen. 'Goed, dan mag u gaan. Nu wil ik daar niets meer van weten!' zei de heer Jaggers, terwijl hij zijn hand op hen uitstak om ze achter zich te plaatsen. 'Als u iets tegen mij zegt, gooi ik de zaak op.' 'We dachten, meneer Jaggers -' begon een van de mannen, terwijl hij zijn hoed afnam. 'Dat is wat ik u niet wilde laten doen,' zei de heer Jaggers. 'Ik denk voor u; dat is genoeg voor u. Als ik u nodig heb, weet ik waar u bent; ik wil niet dat u mij zoekt. Nu wil ik daar niets meer van weten. Ik wil niets horen.' De twee mannen keken elkaar aan terwijl de heer Jaggers hen achter zich plaatste en vielen terug en werden niet meer gehoord.

his room. He led me to a dark room. After I had waited for a long time Mr Jaggers arrived.
Many people, men and women, who had been waiting for him outside the office, made a rush at him. He addressed himself to two of the men.
'Now, I have nothing to say to you,' said Mr Jaggers, pointing his finger at them. 'I want to know no more than I know. As to the result, it could go either way. I told you that from the start. Have you paid Wemmick?'
'Yes, sir,' said both the men together.
'Very well; then you may go. Now, I won't have it!' said Mr Jaggers, waving his hand at them to put them behind him. 'If you say a word to me, I'll throw up the case.'
'We thought, Mr Jaggers -' one of the men began, pulling off his hat.
'That's what I told you not to do,' said Mr Jaggers. 'You thought! I think for you; that's enough for you. If I want you, I know where to find you; I don't want you to find me. Now I won't have it. I won't hear a word.' 
The two men looked at one another as Mr Jaggers waved them behind him, and fell back and were heard no more.

SUNNINGDALE HOTEL

The Sunningdale Hotel was built in 1913 and opened by Princess Louise. It has provided excellent service for people from all over the world and people of all ages and nationalities have stayed here. During the past 80years over 50,000 guests from 174different countries have visited Sunningdale.
The hotel is on one of the main roads leading to the town centre. It is about 20 minutes by bus from the centre of town and buses to many other parts of the town stop outside the hotel. Guests should be careful not to travel on buses with the blue sign Express on the front because they do not stop near our hotel. An underground station is less than 100 metres away.
The main building has 200 well-furnished, centrally-heated single rooms, each fitted with hot and cold water basins. Showers, baths and toilets are at the end of all corridors. The hotel has a shop, sitting rooms, four television rooms, table tennis room, library and laundry. There are also eight pianos available for guests' use. There are spaces to park cars in the hotel drive.
Daily newspapers are provided free and stamps can be bought at the office.Guests who stay for long periods must pay for their accommodation weekly in advance and one week's notice is required for departures. Short or long term guests are welcome but long term guests are offered rooms first.
Meal times are: breakfast 7 am - 9.30 am; lunch 1 pm - 2pm; dinner 5.30pm - 7 pm. During the week, for those studying or working late, dinner can be requested until 11pm by writing your name on the late list or by telephoning before 7 pm. A selection of 10menu choices are available for breakfast and dinner.
No animals of any description or fires of any type (either for heating food or heating the room) are allowed, and guests are requested to respect the comfort of others. If you have tapes or CDs, please try to keep the noise level down to a minimum, especially between the hours of 11pm and 8am.
Guests are advised to use taxis to get to the hotel if they arrive by train because we are some distance from the main railway station.

SUNNINGDALE HOTEL

Het Sunningdale Hotel werd in 1913 gebouwd en geopend door Prinses Louise. Het hotel biedt een uitstekende service aan mensen van over de hele wereld. Mensen van alle leeftijden en nationaliteiten hebben hier verbleven. In de afgelopen 80 jaar hebben meer dan 50.000 gasten uit 174 verschillende landen het Sunningdale Hotel bezocht.

Het hotel ligt aan een van de hoofdwegen naar het centrum van de stad. Het is ongeveer 20 minuten met de bus naar het centrum van de stad en bussen naar veel andere delen van de stad stoppen voor het hotel. Gasten moeten oppassen dat ze niet in bussen stappen met het blauwe bord Express op de voorzijde, omdat deze niet stoppen bij ons hotel. Er is een metrostation op minder dan 100 meter afstand.

Het hoofdgebouw heeft 200 goed ingerichte, centraal verwarmde eenpersoonskamers, elk uitgerust met warm en koud water. Douches, baden en toiletten zijn aan het einde van alle gangen. Het hotel heeft een winkel, zitkamers, vier televisiekamers, een tafeltennistafel, een bibliotheek en een wasserette. Er zijn ook acht piano's beschikbaar voor gebruik door gasten. Er zijn parkeerplaatsen voor auto's in de oprit van het hotel.

Er worden dagelijkse kranten gratis verstrekt en stempels kunnen worden gekocht bij het kantoor. Gasten die langere tijd blijven moeten hun accommodatie wekelijks vooraf betalen en een week van tevoren moet worden opgezegd. Gasten die voor lange of korte tijd verblijven zijn welkom, maar langetermijngasten krijgen eerst een kamer.

De maaltijden zijn: ontbijt van 7.00 tot 9.30 uur, lunch van 13.00 tot 14.00 uur en diner van 17.30 tot 19.00 uur. Tijdens de week kunnen gasten die studeren of werken tot laat, diner bestellen tot 23.00 uur door hun naam op de late lijst te schrijven of voor 19.00 uur te bellen. Er is een selectie van 10 menukeuzes beschikbaar voor ontbijt en diner.

Er zijn geen dieren van welke aard dan ook of vuren toegestaan en gasten worden verzocht het comfort van anderen te respecteren. Als u cassettes of CD's hebt, probeer dan het geluidsniveau tot een minimum te beperken, vooral tussen 23.00 en 8.00 uur.

Gasten worden geadviseerd om een taxi te nemen om naar het hotel te komen als ze met de trein aankomen, omdat het hotel op een afstand ligt van het belangrijkste treinstation.

Charles Darwin (1809-1882) developed a revolutionary theory of evolution that transformed the way we understand the world and we see ourselves. In On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, Darwin described the process of natural selection. 
The 'fittest' animals or plants - those with the characteristics best suited to their environment - are more likely to survive and reproduce. They pass on these desirable characteristics to their offspring. Gradually those features become more common, causing the species to change over time. If the changes are great enough, they can produce an entirely new species. 
The Descent of Man, published in 1871, suggested that humans descended from apes. When Darwin studied medicine, he witnessed an operation performed on a child without anaesthetic. That made him give up medical studies. 
He then studied theology but, instead of becoming a priest, in 1831 he set off on a five-year scientific expedition around the world. There he collected evidence for his future theory. One of the key arguments for natural selection came from the birds that Darwin collected from the Gal pagos Islands. The birds were clearly the same species but some had large strong beaks for eating nuts while others had long thin beaks for finding worms in the ground. 
Darwin realised that all came from a single ancestor but, as they dispersed to different islands, they had adapted to eat the various foods available. Darwin developed the theory of evolution in the 1830s but he didn't announce it then. He knew his ideas were radical so he delayed publishing the theory for about twenty years while he assembled more evidence.

In On the Origin of Species, gepubliceerd in 1859, beschreef Darwin het proces van natuurlijke selectie. De 'best aangepaste' dieren of planten - die de beste eigenschappen hebben voor hun omgeving - hebben meer kans om te overleven en zich voort te planten. Ze geven deze wenselijke eigenschappen door aan hun nakomelingen. Langzaam worden deze kenmerken steeds meer gemeengoed, waardoor de soorten in de loop van de tijd veranderen. Als de veranderingen groot genoeg zijn, kunnen ze een volledig nieuwe soort produceren. In The Descent of Man, gepubliceerd in 1871, suggereerde Darwin dat de mens afstamt van apen. Toen Darwin medicijnen studeerde, was hij getuige van een operatie die werd uitgevoerd op een kind zonder verdoving. Dat zorgde ervoor dat hij zijn medische studies opgaf. Hij studeerde vervolgens theologie, maar in plaats van priester te worden, vertrok hij in 1831 voor een vijfjarige wetenschappelijke expeditie rond de wereld. Daar verzamelde hij bewijs voor zijn toekomstige theorie. Een van de belangrijkste argumenten voor natuurlijke selectie kwam van de vogels die Darwin verzamelde op de Galapagos-eilanden. De vogels waren duidelijk dezelfde soort, maar sommigen hadden grote, sterke snavels om noten te eten, terwijl anderen lange, dunne snavels hadden om wormen in de grond te vinden. Darwin realiseerde zich dat ze allemaal van één voorouder kwamen, maar toen ze zich verspreidden naar verschillende eilanden, hadden ze zich aangepast om het voedsel te eten dat beschikbaar was. Darwin ontwikkelde de theorie van de evolutie in de jaren 1830, maar hij maakte deze toen niet bekend. Hij wist dat zijn ideeën radicaal waren, dus hij liet de theorie twintig jaar lang liggen terwijl hij meer bewijs verzamelde.

In On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, Darwin described the process of natural selection. The 'best adapted' animals or plants - those with the best traits for their environment - are more likely to survive and reproduce. They pass on these desirable traits to their offspring. Slowly, these traits become more common, causing the species to change over time. If the changes are great enough, they can produce an entirely new species. In The Descent of Man, published in 1871, Darwin suggested that humans are descended from apes. When Darwin was studying medicine, he witnessed an operation being performed on a child without anaesthetic. This led him to abandon his medical studies. He then studied theology, but instead of becoming a priest, he set off on a five-year scientific expedition around the world in 1831. There he collected evidence for his future theory. One of the main arguments for natural selection came from the birds that Darwin collected on the Galapagos Islands. The birds were clearly the same species, but some had large, strong beaks for eating nuts, while others had long, thin beaks for finding worms in the ground. Darwin realised that they had all come from one ancestor, but as they spread to different islands, they had adapted to eat the food that was available. Darwin developed the theory of evolution in the 1830s, but he did not make it public at the time. He knew that his ideas were radical, so he left the theory alone for twenty years while he collected more evidence.
